85.Market linkages. Marketing Groups will be supported to enter into productive alliances, PPPs or other types of

contract farming relationships. The service provider will play a brokerage role and actively engage with existing sub-

sector or commodity platforms (for example the rice sector platform which brings value chain actors together); or

support the creation of new partnerships, around prioritized value chains in the irrigation schemes.



Matching grants for value addition and marketing



86.The project will support marketing groups to attain increased commercialization and value addition from the

increased agricultural production, by providing matching grants. The project will provide matching grants to interested

marketing groups, based on a careful selection and assessment of the capacity of the group to utilize the public

investment for maximum long-term gain.



                                           Box 1.3. Matching Grant experiences in MAAIF

 MAAIF has several, varying experiences in the use of matching grants. Some of the most relevant experiences which have

 informed the project design are:

  National Agricultural Advisory Services (NAADS): during FY 2005/06 government provide funding through Integrated

     Support to Farmer Groups, in the form of revolving grants managed at sub-county level. The grant scheme was designed for

     farmer institution development and organization; increasing effective farmer demand for productivity enhancing

     technologies; and increasing farmers’ access to input and product markets through active linkage of farmer groups with

     processors/produce buyers and input stockists. Farmers’ access to production inputs; and value addition and marketing tools,

     equipment and machinery was improved under the grant. The key principles of managing the grant were demand-driven and

     market-oriented production; empowerment, ownership and promoting self – reliance; promoting entrepreneurship and

     innovation; maintaining equitable access to the grant; and linkage with research for technology development.

  JICA has through several smaller projects provided grants (with and without matching contributions from farmers) mainly in

     the rice sub-sector. The observed productivity and value addition benefits have not been observed and there has been limited

     maintenance and thus limited lifespan of the machinery / processing equipment provided. The presence of any grant element,

     even if matched, has been found to create adverse effects. JICA no longer provides grants or matching grants to inputs or

     agro-processing or other inputs.

  FIEFOC provides grants to the specific groups which have been trained by the project; no matching contribution from the

     farmers in envisaged as they are selected based on demonstrated willingness and commitment on ground. Goods are either

     bulk procured or funds disbursed to FGs on ground and spent on post-harvest handling equipment, small equipment, rice

     threshers, rippers, hullers etc thought community procurement. A special youth incubator and investment fund is established

     providing dedicated business plan development, validation, grants for investment and mentoring to ensure usage of the grant

     finance in accordance with the business plan.

  ACDP envisages to provide matching grants to HLFOs, following a graduation of farmers’ groups approaches. The grant may

     be up to US$7,000, with 67 percent of the investment financed by the project and 33 percent matched by the farmer. Co-

     financing is assessed through on-the-ground verification of e.g. cash, bricks or land, and the grant disbursed directly to the

     farmer group to be used through community procurement processes. No grants have yet been disbursed.



87.The activities are designed in accordance with lessons learnt from other projects, namely: (i) distribution of free

inputs or equipment does not necessarily lead to intended results; (ii) identification of high-potential and serious

farmers, one needs regular and hands-on engagement on ground; (iii) matching grants should only be provided through

strong, commercially-oriented groups, which have good governance and business-plans which clearly demonstrates

willingness and ability to operate and maintain equipment; and (iv) the modality for matching contributions from groups

may need to be flexible, and may include both cash or in-kind contributions.

text:
(US$20.19 million equivalent)

29.      This component supports to improve efficiency, accountability and citizen engagement in the delivery

of selected services by Selected Entities. There are four major sets of constraints to service delivery

improvements, namely (a) upstream challenges, including lack of streamlined and standardized systems and

processes for service delivery and results tracking, and inadequate and unpredictable budget releases for goods

and services; (b) downstream challenges, including limited access points and insufficient MDA institutional

capacity to formulate and manage efficient and accountable processes at the point of service to citizens and firms;

(c) horizontal challenges including limited coordination between sector MDAs; and (d) delays, corruption, lack of

complaints handling and tracking mechanisms and a general lack of public accountability and citizen engagement

pertaining to key public services, across MDAs.

title: Digital financial inclusion (US$28 million equivalent)
text:
25. The objective of this component is to stimulate the use of digital financial services in rural areas, primarily through

    mobile money, for promoting financial inclusion with particular emphasis on women and youth, and thus contribute

    to improve the well-being of rural population and economic development. The project will focus on selected high-

    priority, high impact and sustainable initiatives that: a) will foster the development and the adoption of digital

    financial services; b) complement current ongoing activities to support financial inclusion including the FIRST

    financial inclusion program in Niger, and the PIMELAN project recently approved and aiming at expanding access to

    financial services, such as credit, insurance, savings; c) allow inclusion of vulnerable populations and refugees

    receiving safety nets under existing World Bank programs and are achievable within the allocated timeframe and

    budget; and d) help to mobilize Niger's digital ecosystem and seek to develop financial inclusion and key services in

    important sectors for rural areas, in particular agriculture. Special attention will be given to the development of

    synergies with the World Bank projects in Niger which will benefit both to the Component 3 and to the projects. The

    projects identified and potential areas of synergy are described in Table 1.2 in Annex 1.

26. As a result of the COVID-19 pandemic, every effort will be made to accelerate the roll-out of the activities planned

    under Component 3, and to tailor them to respond to the crisis recovery period. Specific activities planned in this

    context include:

       a. Mobile money literacy campaigns;

       b. Facilitating delivery of social safety nets to vulnerable populations via mobile phones;

       c. Expansion of grants to merchants in rural and rural areas so that they can accept mobile money to reduce cash

          manipulation and liquidity crunch;

       d. Support to FINTECH companies to facilitate delivery of microloans, micro-insurance products;

       e. Support for use of geospatial data to optimize the delivery of cash transfers and financial services; and

       f. Support to facilitate interoperability between mobile money operators.

27. According to recent World Bank studies32, main reasons of the limited uptake of mobile finance in Niger include:

     a. Weak network coverage and lack of interoperability. At least 10 percent of Niger’s population is not covered even

        by a 2G mobile network. While 2G allows mobile finance through Unstructured Supplementary Service Data

        (USSD), the speed is inadequate for large-scale mobile finance and does not allow data coverage, which is needed

        to give users access to better digital finance solutions that use smartphones or require data exchange for example.

        Furthermore, there is a lack of interconnection among operators which constrains users to conduct cash in/cash

        out only with operators they are registered with. This is a real issue, especially in rural areas given the limited

        presence of mobile money agents.







32

     Digitalization of Government Payments.







                                                                                                                        Page 55 of 89


           The World Bank

           Niger: Smart Villages for Rural Growth and Digital Inclusion Project (P167543)





     b. Inadequacy of digital financial services offers and solutions tailored to the needs of the population. Existing

        digital financial solutions are out of reach of a large share of the population. The main reason is that the content

        is mainly in French, whereas only one fifth of the Niger population are literate in French (compared to more than

        half that speak Hausa and one fifth that speak Songhai33). Most of the non-francophone users have to rely on their

        friends and family to conduct even basic digital transactions. This triggers some trust, security, and convenience

        issues. Also, as mentioned above, the scarcity of information about the usage patterns of the rural population

        makes it difficult for financial intermediaries to design appropriate products for them.

     c. An unconducive ecosystem for digital finance characterized by a low density of mobile money agents, limited

        opportunities for usage of mobile money, and stiff competition from informal payment service providers. There

        are 17 mobile money outlets per 1,000 km2 in Niger. Only 38 percent of them are active, which is both the lowest

        rate and absolute number among WAEMU countries, with the exception of Guinea Bissau. Many of the active

        mobile money agents have liquidity issues which is reflected in their limited capacities to do cash out transactions.

        The inability of people to withdraw money from their mobile money accounts, for instance due to shortage of

        currency in rural areas, highly influences the lack of trust in mobile money and encourages potential users to rely

        more on payment service providers – over-the-counter (OTC) channels and informal payments services – for cash

        transfers.

     d. Limited opportunity to use mobile money. Evidence show that options of payments through mobile are now

        offered by the utility companies, but there are only 44 registered businesses and shops that accept mobile

        payments, and most of them are inactive. In addition to these constraints, there is also the taxation on mobile

        money agents’ services, newly introduced, which will ultimately increase the price to consumers of mobile finance.

     e. Low awareness, low digital literacy, low financial literacy and limited trust. While there is a growing sense that

        access to financial account is important, there is a very limited awareness of mobile money accounts, and of the

        possible uses of these accounts, due to lack of digital financial literacy in general. Lack of digital literacy and lack

        of connectivity create additional trust issues.

     f.   Limited trust between mobile operators and some financial sector players. Many of the financial intermediaries

          prefer to develop their own digital solutions rather than partnering with mobile operators. The Post Office,

          ECOBANK, BOA for example are putting in place their own digital platforms for digital financial services with

          technology providers. Bad experiences of some of these financial intermediaries with some mobile operators have

          contributed to reduce the level of trust. Furthermore, the decision of one of the operators to become a bank has

          reduced the desire of financial intermediaries to enter in partnerships with mobile operators.

28. Fortunately, there are multiple ongoing initiatives that are not only contributing to address some of these challenges

    but are also creating a strong momentum around digital finance:

     a. Niger has revised its financial inclusion strategy to put a stronger emphasis on digital finance with the support of

        development partners including the World Bank.

     b. The Government is preparing the ground for the digitization of its payments. It has already interfaced its

        information system with the regional payment infrastructure35, that reduces turnaround time from several weeks

        to a day at most. An inter-ministerial committee was created, with the support of the World Bank under the FIRST

        Financial Inclusion program, to develop a strategy and a roadmap for the digitization of Government payments

        (G2P and P2G payments).

     c. Digital literacy training has been launched by ANSI since 2017 to raise women’s awareness of digital

        transformation, albeit at very small scale.

     d. A business plan competition (i-TAKARA) was launched to support digital entrepreneurship and digital innovation,

        and this has demonstrated an increasing level of interest of youth and women to embrace digital transformation

        and to play a key role in the process.

     e. Some women associations are using WhatsApp to collect money in the context of informal savings groups

        (tontines) and NGO CARE is digitizing VSLAs in the country that gathered more than 600,000 women with the

        objective to link them with formal financial institutions.

29. The proposed activities under this component are focused on building a digital ecosystem in rural areas, specifically

    in the Smart Villages, by digitizing some key payments received or made by the rural population and facilitating the

    use of mobile money accounts through targeted accompanying measures including financial education and digital

    literacy. In addition, this digitization will be complemented by the creation of a data platform on agricultural

    producers, including an e-KYC registry, with a view to facilitating their future access to credit from financial



35 Within the West Africa region, an inter-bank payments system is provided by the WAEMU Automated Interbank Clearing System (SICA-UEMOA,

in French) for smaller amounts and a regional gross settlement system (STAR-UEMOA) for larger amounts.

       Niger: Smart Villages for Rural Growth and Digital Inclusion Project (P167543)





    institutions. Thereby, by facilitating the use of mobile money accounts among rural population, the project will lay

    the groundwork for broader financial inclusion via traditional financial institutions (banks and MFIs) allowing access

    to more diversified financial services beyond payments such as savings, credit and insurance.

30. Sub‐component 3.1. Creating digital centers and improving the digital ecosystem (US$13.5 million) – This

    component will address the lack of financial literacy, lack of agents, and will improve acceptance of digital payments

    by merchants. Currently in rural Niger, most people do not have access to formal financial services and have a poor

    understanding of digital financial services, especially women. The digital ecosystem is underdeveloped and there are

    few or none use cases for the use of e-money. In addition, mobile money agents are rare or have difficulties to face

    cash out because of an insufficient working capital and limited incentive due to limited volume of mobile money

    activities in the current situation. To face these barriers, the project will support three main activities:

31. Activity 3.1.1. Creation of digital centers network in rural areas – It is expected that the project will support the

    creation of 150 multi services digital centers by providing sub-grants for improvement of existing premises to house

    the centers, providing working capital (in the form of grants), training for the managers of the centers and helping

    to develop a business model that could allow the center to be sustainable even after the closing of the project. These

    centers will complement the existing mobile money agents in the targeted areas and will help fill the gaps while

    bringing additionality through more intensive support to customers. A competitive process through a call for

    proposals to be launched by the PIU will allow to select three companies that will have the responsibility to select

    and manage the centers, and the sub-grants they would receive. The profile of the companies will have to comply

    with specific requirements including experience in running a network of points of service, an existing activity in rural

    areas, a knowledge of money transfer activities. These companies will receive sub-grants under the project (i) to

    acquire, upgrade, and maintain digital centers in the villages; (ii) cover their operational expenses; and (iii) develop

    business models that could allow the digital center to be sustainable even after the closing of this project. The

    companies will be selected through a competitive bidding process. Preference will be given to public or private

    companies with existing premises in rural areas. Most of the services delivered in the centers will be free of charge

    for the rural populations except for power for mobile charging, and transaction fees for cash-out. To ensure

    affordability of these fees, the project will work with mobile finance providers to develop more attractive cost

    structure for cash-out transactions.

32. Activity 3.1.2. Digital financial literacy programs. The project will finance digital financial literacy campaigns and

    consumer protection programs including related apps. For that, the project will work with NGOs, women associations

    and religious and traditional leaders to address trust, social and cultural barriers. The deployment of these education

    campaigns will be carried out in local languages, will use a variety of multimedia (images, comics, local radio stations

    etc.), social media channels (WhatsApp messages, etc. ...), and will be combined with face to face engagements in

    the digital centers. Special attention will be given to the development of content relevant for women.

33. Activity 3.1.3. Improving acceptance of digital payments by merchants – The acceptance by merchants of digital

    payments essentially requires, in partnership with MNOs or with aggregators, information, awareness and training

    campaigns as well as attractive cost option compared to cash transactions (see activity 3.2.3). An analysis of the rural

    merchants’ value chain will also be needed to understand what incentives could motivate these merchants to

    willingly accept digital payments. Payment devices with integrated contactless payment solutions will preferred to

    facilitate usage by the rural populations. Preference will be given to merchants in regions and communes around

    smart villages. The eligibility criteria to receive payment devices will be further defined in the operation manual

    based on the results of the analysis on the rural merchants.

title: Digitizing payments and development of new fintech products
text:
32. This sub-component will comprise (i) digitizing payments made and received by farmers; and (ii) promoting new digital

    financial products for women and farmers.

33. To accelerate digitizing payments made and received by farmers, the project will support:

     a. Activity 3.2.1. Digitization of payments received by the public agriculture input supplier, Nigerien Association

        Responsible for Agricultural Inputs (CAIMA) or large input suppliers - This will be done by financing the upgrading

        the back-end processes (Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) system) and financing 75 percent of the costs of

        payment devices for wholesalers and their retailers to allow them to receive digital payments from farmers.

        b. Activity 3.2.2. Digitization of payments made to farmers - This will be done by financing the creation of an ERP

           solution and other payment infrastructure to enable five agriculture federations to manage the constituency of

           co-operatives and for the co-operatives in turn to manage the farmers under them. Priority will be given to

           agriculture federations in the value chains with a high number of members in communes and regions around smart

           villages, and to value chains supported by other World Bank projects including the Agriculture and Transformation

           project Agricultural and Livestock Transformation Program (PIMELAN, (P164509) or other donors to ensure

           synergies.

        c. Activity 3.2.3. Promoting new digital finance products for farmers and women - The project will offer sub-grants

           of up to a maximum amount of US$250,00021, through a business competition plan to Fintech companies, and

           startups. The sub-grants will cover seed funding, operation costs, costs for piloting new digital financial and non-

           financial solutions for women and farmers for two years. Priority will be given to Fintech or startups which will

           develop business models around saving groups. Fintech and start-ups companies (local, regional or international)

           interested in entering or expanding their activities in Niger will be eligible to receive the sub-grants. Also, to be

           eligible to receive sub-grants for the piloting of new solutions, the Fintech and startups will have to demonstrate

           that there is not yet a clear business case (e.g. serving those populations that are unlikely to be profitable in the

           first two years). The grantee will be encouraged to partner with financial institutions or similar institutions in Niger

           to offer financial services.

title: Creating a digital data platform to enable access by rural populations to formal accounts and
text:
increase access to better-suited financial services (US$6.9 million). This sub-component aims at developing a data

    platform on agricultural producers (farmers and livestock breeders) including an e-KYC registry to facilitate their

    future access to additional financial services beyond payment services, in particular access to credit. The vast

    majority of agricultural producers do not currently have an account in a financial institution (Bank or MFI) and

    therefore do not access formal savings, credit or insurance services. Financial institutions have so far shown limited

    interest in this segment of the population due in particular to lack of available and workable information which the

    creation of this data platform is intended to fill. The project activities will enable and facilitate access to the mobile

    money account for payment and money transfer services, the first step to financial inclusion, but producers' needs

    go beyond. The creation of a data platform on producers will prepare this second step towards access to savings and

    especially credit from financial institutions.

42. Traditionally, credit history is based on data provided by lenders. While this method has been reliably used, it is

    simply inadequate in the present day for Niger as it captures only information on thin segment of the populations

    which has already access to credit

43. The project intends to collect data of various types including information on: personal situation, agricultural and

    non-agricultural activities including their geolocation (tool like Google plus addresses could be used), financial

    transactions carried out on the Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) system. The digital platform will work by

    partnering with a network of digitally-enabled partners including mobile operators, farmers organizations with a

    focus on women’s formal and informal organizations (including the VSLAs supported by NGO CARE), payment service

    providers (banks, microfinance institutions, remittances providers) to collect information that could be used for

    credit scoring.

44. The collection of data with producers will be coordinated with the “Basic Biometric Identification System” activity

    from the West Africa Unique Identification for Regional Integration and Inclusion Program (WURI, P161328)

    supported by the World Bank in order to ensure that producers will already have a unique ID number that will be

    associated with their data.

45. The design of the data platform will be compliant with the national and WAEMU legal and regulatory provisions on

    protection of personal data. In agreement with ANSI, the data platform will be hosted at the Central Bank (BCEAO).

    The manager of the data platform, a separate entity, will have to be completely independent, present no conflict of

    interest and shall comply with current data protection regulations and BCEAO requirements in order to ensure

    confidence among financial services providers and other entities.

46. Activity 3.3.1. Data collection will be done during the whole implementation of the project, but initial data collection

    will be carried out by consulting firms to be recruited by the project in close collaboration with CAIMA retailers,

    Maisons du paysans, agriculture cooperatives, CARE NGO, and the World Bank projects on safety nets and

    agriculture. Based on a call for proposals, a firm (or several depending of capacities) will be recruited to collect data

    in the villages and to train local authorities to continue this work at the end of the project to ensure sustainability.



                                                                                                                Page 61 of 89


       The World Bank

       Niger: Smart Villages for Rural Growth and Digital Inclusion Project (P167543)





    The firm will manage field staff that will be trained. The data collection will involve the local administrative and

    traditional authorities who will help inform and sensitize producers to adhere to the project and share their data.

47. Activity 3.3.2. Creation of a digital data platform, which will comprise a credit scoring system and e-KYC registry.

    The project will hire firms to design the digital data platform. Before, a study will need to be done to identify and

    assess existing platforms and apps and see how to build on these platforms. The credit scoring system will allow to

    collect alternative data (personal and farm information, social network behavior, financial transactions done through

    mobile money accounts and other platforms) to be used for credit scoring purposes and to help create better suited

    financial products to the needs of rural populations. The e-KYC registry (detailed in Box 3) will allow to have

    centralized KYC information on their customers and help financial institutions comply with Customer Due Diligence

    (CDD) regulation which constitute a key component for compliance with Anti-Money Laundering and Combatting

    the Financing of Terrorism (AML/CFT) requirements.

                                                Figure 2: Digital data platform









48. Activity 3.3.3. The project will also create simple apps so that users could themselves update their profile on their

    cell phones.

49. Activity 3.3.4. Interface of the data platform with participating financial institutions, and existing and to be created

    platforms. Existing platforms to be connected to include participating financial institutions systems, mobile devices,

    agriculture payments platforms (to be put in place under Sub-component 2) so that all data related to the purchase

    of air time, mobile money transfers, purchase of inputs and selling of their products via mobile services.

50. Activity 3.3.5. Technical support for the implementation of the digital data platform. This will include (i) the design

    of algorithms for credit scoring that could be used by participating financial institutions; (ii) the training and on-

    boarding of the participating financial institutions, BCEAO, the manager of the platform and other stakeholders; (iii)

    the design of the business model to ensure financial viability of the platform, and supervisory frameworks for the

    development of a data platform covering credit scoring and an e-KYC registry.

 Box 4: Towards an e-KYC (Know-Your-Customer) registry



 To facilitate the opening of accounts in financial institutions for financially excluded populations, this digital

 data platform will host an e-KYC (Know-Your-Customer) registry. The registry will help financial institutions to

 identify their customers and comply with Customer Due Diligence (CDD) regulation which constitute a key





                                                                                                              Page 62 of 89


      The World Bank

      Niger: Smart Villages for Rural Growth and Digital Inclusion Project (P167543)





component for compliance with AML/CFT requirements. Indeed, high costs incurred by complex and time-

consuming KYC controls and diligences are often considered as main barriers to financial inclusion. These costs

are likely to keep financial institutions from providing financial services to the disadvantaged population which

may not be considered sufficiently profitable. Recognizing this critical issue, the G20 High Level Principles on

Digital Financial Inclusion issued by the Global Partnership for Financial Inclusion (GPFI) in 2016 included the

need to facilitate customer ID for digital financial services as a key pillar for financial inclusion under its principle

7.



The e-KYC platform intends to help authorities of Niger to comply with this principle, by designing and providing

an e-KYC registry which will facilitate the ID process of customers (whether permanent of occasional, and

whether natural or legal person), the verification of customer’s identity, and the implementation of on-going

customer monitoring.



In addition, supervisors will also take benefit of the information stored in the e-KYC registry which may facilitate

their controls (on documentary fraud or suspicious activity reports for instance). This registry could lead the

supervisors to adjust their internal procedures in terms of controls and propose legal amendments to the

AML/CFT law if necessary, contributing therein to the implementation of an effective AML/CFT risk-based

supervisory approach.



From a technical point of view, this e-KYC registry may take different forms and will have to be adapted to the

Nigerien context after considering the main conclusions issued by the WBG Policy Note on e-KYC registries that

is currently being finalized, as well as knowledge about all potential tools existing on the market. However, as

potential characteristics (provided below only as examples and close to the Indian model), the e-KYC registry

could enable new clients to submit directly on the digital platform a dully filled and signed KYC form (with

supporting documents to verify proof of identity and proof of address and potentially linked to digital ID) before

being allotted via SMS or email a single digit KYC ID number (KIN) which would need to be quoted by the client

while conducting any financial transaction. For existing clients, financial institutions could be able to submit

directly on the platform the required documents using bulk upload or file transfer mechanisms. The technical

modalities of access of the e-KYC registry by the financial institutions will have to be determined by the

technological solutions’ provider.



The e-KYC registry will be applicable in the first place only to individuals (population of Smart Villages) but could

be extended to the entire population of Niger in the medium term. The authorities will have to define the

business model of the e-KYC registry, as to whether it should be financially sustainable (charging fees for

financial institutions or/and administrative or judicial authorities to access the data) or encourage financial

inclusion through the covering by the national budget of the maintenance costs.



According to a new regulation that will have to be adopted by the Minister of Finance before the creation of

the e-KYC registry, the digital data platform held by ANSI will receive, store, safeguard and retrieve KYC records

in a digital form for every client of financial institutions. The bidders will propose the best technological

                                          ANNEX 2: Economic and Financial Analysis



1. The scope of the connectivity activity in Component 2 (i.e. extending digital connectivity to targeted rural areas)

   involves the construction of a digital infrastructure in the rural and remote parts of Niger to cover the targeted

   villages. According to the ANSI, there are around 500,000 inhabitants in the 2,111 targeted villages that are not

   covered by any mobile signal. The construction of the digital infrastructure will allow for an important expansion in

   the provision of mobile telephony services and mobile broadband services to citizens and smallholders. This is

   particularly crucial in closing the gender gap in mobile phone ownership/ usage, where women are not covered by

   mobile signal in their home/village but are not allowed to leave it.

2. The financial and economic analysis of the project is based on the incremental approach37. All cash flows are stated

   in constant US$. The reference period is set equal to the standard lifecycle period for a digital infrastructure (i.e. 20

   years) and thus no residual value is considered at the end of the reference period.



3. Component 2 – The project is viable financially and economically

     a. The results for the project without public capital support are: (i) the Financial Rate of Return FRR(C) is 7 percent;

        (ii) the break-even point occurs in 15 years; and (iii) the NPV is -US$22.7 million (with a discount rate of 10

        percent). These results show that although FRR(C) is positive, telecommunication operators would not invest in

        this project alone because it would not provide the minimum rate of return that private mobile operator

        companies usually expect (around 12 to 16 percent depending on the socio-economic context). Therefore, public

        Government financing is needed to make the project possible.

     b. The results for the project with public capital support are: (i) the Financial Rate of Return FRR(K) is 14 percent;

        (ii) the break-even point occurs in 12 years; and (iii) the Net Present Value NPV(K) is US$23.8 million (with a

        discount rate of 10 percent). These results show that the project becomes acceptable for private operators.

        Moreover, the fact that after taking into account the public capital, the Financial Rate of Return FRR(K) is in the

        average of the expected rate of return for standard mobile telecommunications projects and that the break-

        even point occurs in the long-term (12 years) show that the public capital support is not over-proportionate.

     c. Although last-mile operators were consulted in advance, there is a high level of uncertainty with regards to the

        revenues that will be generated by the infrastructure. This is acknowledged in the design of the project, which

        requires the inclusion of a claw-back mechanism into the PPP contract that would apply in case revenues are

        higher than originally foreseen.

     d. A sensitivity analysis is performed on the assumptions for the supply-side (unit cost of a site and OPEX as a

        percentage rate of CAPEX), the demand-side (penetration rate and ARPU), and the discount factor. It shows that

        the business model is sensitive to the assumptions and could be overly profitable, thus reinforcing the need of a

        claw-back mechanism.

     e. The economic analysis can be performed on a macroeconomic level (estimate the local GDP growth generated

        by additional mobile and broadband users) or a microeconomic level (such as household consumer surplus or

        time and cost savings derived from the use of online services). However, the economic analysis cannot be

        performed by using these methods due to: (i) the coverage expansion areas (white zones) being scattered rather

    guidelines acceptable to the World Bank for implementing the project CERC activities will be prepared

     Project Beneficiaries

    50.     The project is expected to benefit directly and indirectly all economic agents in the project areas

    operating along the targeted value chains from production to market, including at the processing,

    storage, transport and trading stages. The total number of project beneficiaries is estimated in the order

    of 150,000 individuals.

    51.      Direct project beneficiaries are first and foremost all the smallholder crop farmers, processors,

    traders and marketers who will be involved in project-supported activities at farm-gate level and

    downstream of production. These include prominently the smallholders and entrepreneurs who will

    benefit from irrigation development, extension and subsidy for the new technology packages, and the

    project matching grants as part of project financing windows. Other direct beneficiaries will include: (i)

    the staff of MAAH agricultural extension support services and other services directly targeted by project

    activities who will receive technical support and training, and (ii) the off-takers and transporters who will

    use the purchasing counters, and tracks and roads. The project will mainstream gender and youth

    dimensions in all its activities, giving them preferential treatment particularly in project-provided

    agriculture training and services, as well as funding of investment initiatives. This will be achieved by

    targeting economic activities in which women and youth predominate. These include small-scale agro-

    processing activities such as mango drying, and activities in value chains dominated by women such as

    shea nut collection and processing. Youth will be targeted for any project activities focused on training

title: Improvement of Infrastructure and Water Management (US$153.4 million equivalent from IDA)
text:
26.      The primary goal of this component is to contribute to more sustainable and equitable regional water

      resources management in addition to an improved irrigation development in the Logone valley, building upon

      the work done within the recently closed emergency PULCI Project. This will be achieved by combining

      infrastructure, institutional, and informational activities so that SEMRY becomes a modern water institution. The

      component is organized in three subcomponents: (i) upstream water resources monitoring and coordination as

      well as operation and safety of the main hydraulic infrastructure; (ii) rehabilitation of the eight irrigation and

      drainage schemes; and (iii) irrigation and drainage management. First, a water resources unit and WUA oversight

      unit with full Global Information System (GIS) and technical capabilities will be established within SEMRY which

      will be used for land tenure rights management as well. Second, the full rehabilitation of the irrigation schemes

      will need to be undertaken before the transfer of their operation and maintenance to the WUAs. Third, PLL of

      all 12,210 hectares will be carried out to enhance water use efficiency and enable private sector-led land

      preparation and mechanized paddy cultivation operations. It is also expected that extensive training of the WUAs

      will be needed, and transfer agreements between SEMRY and the WUAs will be put in place. This component

      will finance studies, consulting services, works, equipment, and training.

text:
47. Following an eligible crisis or emergency, the Borrower may request the World Bank to re-allocate

        project funds to support emergency response and reconstruction. This component would draw from the

        uncommitted credit resources under the project from other project components to cover the emergency

        response.

C. Project Beneficiaries

        48.     Different groups of poor people can be expected to benefit from increases in agricultural productivity

        from the Logone Valley irrigation project. Poor farmers, particularly women farmers, will benefit from higher

        incomes brought about by the ability to increase irrigation productivity and a likely doubling of cropping

        intensity (to 180 percent) from the current very low land utilization on the schemes (only one crop per year).

        Productivity gains in irrigation farming will lead to ripple-effect benefits in the form of local economic activity

        for agricultural services (land preparation, farm mechanization, transport, input-supplies, milling, and

        marketing), and increased food availability at reduced prices, particularly during the dry season. When

        increased agricultural productivity leads to increases in food production, lower food prices will directly benefit

        the (non-farming) urban poor and net food buyers in rural areas who are the poorest in Cameroon. This is not

        inconsequential as high transportation costs to the Far North make food an imperfectly tradeable commodity.

        An important transmission mechanism from agricultural productivity to aggregate growth is through the price

        of food, as it allows lower labor costs in the rest of the economy to be sustained. Through infrastructure

        investments and support for intensifying production, the project will benefit more than 30,000 direct

        beneficiaries (via improved irrigation and drainage) and around 200,000 indirect beneficiaries. In addition,

        improved flood management, including the early warning system, would benefit an estimated 600,000

        residents of the Logone Valley, both in Cameroon and Chad, extending all the way to Lake Chad. Benefits would

        be through an increase in flood preparedness of Government and of the wider population, and reduction in the

        loss of life from flood events.

title: Irrigation and Drainage Infrastructure, and Resettlement Action Plans (RAP) and
text:
Environmental and Social Impact Assessment (ESIA) activities (US$146.5 million from IDA). The pumped

Yagoua area (SEMRY I) consists of four major irrigation schemes totaling around 5,726 ha. The gravity-fed Maga

area (SEMRY II) consists of four major irrigation schemes totaling around 6,484 ha that are supplied by water

from the Maga dam. This subcomponent aims at completing the rehabilitation of the irrigation and drainage

infrastructures for the irrigation perimeters (Yagoua and Maga) for a total of 12,210 ha including PLL. These

activities have the potential to realize energy efficiency gains from improved pumping and locking with the

continued use of zero-emissions gravity-fed systems, particularly in Maga. The emergency project (PULCI)

targeted rehabilitation of various elements with a priority on the bulk-supply system, including the Maga dam

and Logone dike, and some irrigation infrastructure (approximately 15 percent of the irrigation area). The

responsibilities for operation and maintenance of the irrigation and drainage infrastructure will be transferred

to the WUAs in two stages: (i) co-management stage from the validation of the Scheme Management Code -

disbursement condition for this subcomponent- until finalization of works rehabilitation and (ii) full transfer from

the signature of the Transfer Agreement (upon finalization of the works rehabilitation) onwards.

29.      The project design adopts a socio-technical modernization approach in conjunction with Subcomponent

1.3. This involves not only rehabilitation, but where necessary would introduce appropriate infrastructure to

enable and strengthen the practical aspects of irrigation and drainage management under the new institutional

arrangements. This requires the establishment of suitably sized, financially viable, and autonomous (technical)

hydraulic units for the self-governing WUAs to be established under Subcomponent 1.3. Hydraulic structures will

also be needed to enable practical and enforceable distribution modalities within the boundary of the WUA area

of operation. In addition, the rehabilitation will include a review of the intakes from the Logone River, particularly

pumping station number 4 and Djafga. The large sedimentation rates in the Logone river, and the significant

silting up of the left bank near the pumping station 4 (SP4) outlet prevent sufficient access to water for the station

SP4 each year, despite the clearing work undertaken at the start of each dry season (DS). Thus, the pumping

station SP4 will be properly relocated. Funds would be provided for infrastructure rehabilitation and supervision.

30.      The activities associated with the environmental and social management plan (ESMP) of this

subcomponent, such as the re-vegetation of the riverbanks, will be financed as services by the project. This

subcomponent will also support the implementation of the RAP and ESIA activities. The contractor of works, as

part of his duties, will be in charge of their timely implementation.

31.     The rehabilitation includes PLL of the 12,210 hectares of irrigation schemes (within the rehabilitation

contract) because currently the fields are highly unlevelled which, inter alia, results in: (i) huge wastage of

precious and scarcely available irrigation water; (ii) inefficiency of other agricultural inputs, i.e. seed, fertilizers,

herbicides, labor, machinery, etc.; and (iii) dismally low agricultural productivity. Further, the unlevelled fields

pose enormous restrictions for carrying out land preparation operations with normal agricultural tractors and

small machinery/implements, as it is nearly impossible to uniformly apply pre-ploughing soil-softening irrigation

across the irrigation perimeter to enable use of such machines/equipment.

title: Irrigation and Drainage Management (US$5.4 million from IDA). This
text:
subcomponent will include TA and equipment for the WUAs. It will build upon the process of irrigation

management that started within the PULCI project: eight WUAs are already in place (one for every irrigation

scheme), eight meeting rooms have been built and equipped for the WUAs as well as eight warehouses for the

Cooperatives. A Scheme Management Code has been elaborated, and needs approval by MINADER before works

start, that sets out the basic rules concerning: (i) irrigation aspects of the land tenure arrangements and usufruct

rights of women farmers; (ii) WUA rights and duties; (iii) WUA legal/financial oversight; (iv) infrastructure

rehabilitation and transfer agreements; (v) rights and duties of the parties; (vi) a dispute resolution mechanism;

(vii) WUA membership criteria (inclusion of women based on usufruct); and (viii) targets for female leadership in

WUAs. The scheme management code equally includes actions to promote women’s representation in WUAs,

particularly in decision-making positions. These actions include awareness raising on the importance and

benefits of women’s participation/leadership in WUAs and training of female farmers in technical and leadership

skills to facilitate their participation in WUA technical and leadership functions. The transfer process is planned

in two stages: (i) co-management from the signature of the Scheme Management Code until finalization of works

rehabilitation and (ii) full transfer from the signature of the Transfer Agreement (upon finalization of the works

rehabilitation) onwards.

33.       This subcomponent will provide TA and training to SEMRY and WUAs, including inter alia: (i) the

development and update by SEMRY of the list of land users; (ii) preparation and implementation of transfer

agreements between SEMRY and WUAs; (iii) the organization of the distribution of fees (irrigation service fee to

be kept by the WUA, fee for technical support for SEMRY, and land preparation services by the private sector);

(iv) training in good practices of irrigation scheduling with targets and outreach measures to ensure participation

of female farmers; (v) strengthening the capacities of each WUA (including a secretary/accountant and a water

operator technician); (vi) the organization of awareness campaigns for community members on health (e.g.

water-borne diseases) on benefits of equal access to and education for boys and girls and on economic and food

security gains from increasing women farmer’s access to land, water, extension, tools and inputs and education

with targets and outreach measures to ensure participation of women farmers; (vii) support for the

implementation and respect of the Scheme Management Code and the rules of procedure; and (viii) providing

equipment to WUAs and their facilities. A WUA manual will be elaborated for ensuring the support to each of

the eight WUAs. In addition, the TA will also work with the various ministries involved in the elaboration and

updated of an appropriate legal framework for irrigation management at national level. These management

activities will help ensure that the Borrower will have the ability to manage climate change-related droughts,

floods, and sedimentation.

title: Matching Grants for Production and Agribusiness in the Valley (US$9.4 million, of
text:
which US$6.8 million from IDA [US$5.2 million for the Matching Grants themselves and US$1.6 million for

consulting services, equipment and operations] and US$2.0 million from beneficiaries). This subcomponent will

finance: (a) Provision of Matching Grants to Matching Grant Beneficiaries, as further detailed in the Matching

Grants Manual, to support activities related to, inter alia, agricultural production, mechanization, agricultural

value addition, and commercialization. Matching Grants will be provided to producer organizations, associations,

cooperatives, entrepreneurial farmers, and established agribusinesses or startups through three grant windows

tailored to achieve specific outcomes in terms of improving production, value addition, commercialization, and

charge, among others, of the training of the local service providers for ensuring the quality of business plans.

These activities will help promote crop diversification, including promoting perennial crops that act as carbon

sinks, while also promoting efficient water use in the face of water shortages exacerbated by climate change.

The consultant, under the supervision of the Gender Specialist of the PIU, will coordinate with local non-

governmental organizations (NGOs), women associations, and women farmers groups to inform women about

the Matching Grants, and how to seek support, and assist the groups in the development of business plans.

Matching grant implementation will start as soon as the project becomes effective.

title: Strengthening Urban Management (US$35 million equivalent)
text:
22.      This component will strengthen the institutional capacity of all participating LGAs on core urban management

functions and their capacity for sustainable delivery of urban infrastructure and services. It aims to strengthen urban

management in five thematic areas, including urban finance, urban planning and enforcement, urban service delivery and

operations and maintenance, urban resilience, and economic competitiveness. The work builds on earlier technical

assistance and investment support received under ULGSP and TSCP. The objective of the work is to deepen the capacity

building and institutional strengthening activities in those beneficiary cities and to extend the support to new LGAs that

are included in the project, and which did not previously have World Bank support. The institutional strengthening

activities will improve the capacity of LGAs to mobilize own-source revenues, develop and implement responsive service-

delivery arrangements and prepare appropriate planning tools to manage urban growth, reduce exposure to natural

hazards and support local economic development.



23.       Key activities under the five themes include:



      (a) Urban finance activities will build on work started under TSCP and DMDP that set up the Local Government

          Revenue Collection Information System (LGRCIS), which enabled a 457 percent increase in own source revenue

          collection in participating LGAs from 2010-2020. TACTIC will finance TA to continue: (i) collection, processing, and

          use of revenue collection data; (ii) development and operationalization of Revenue Enhancement Strategies and

          capacity building in procurement and financial management; (iii) strengthening of financial management in areas

          flagged in annual CAG reports; (iv) the refinement and operationalization of new functions of the Local

          Government Revenue Collection Information System (LGRCIS). Activities will include equipment and training at

          the LGA level, as well as sensitization and training to strengthen monitoring, supervision, and technical assistance

          provided by the regional and ministerial levels to further enhance LGA performance;

      (b) Urban planning and enforcement activities will focus on: (i) preparing land use and infrastructure plans for LGAs

          which currently lack them; and (ii) strengthening LGA capacity to protect infrastructure rights-of-way and

          environmentally sensitive lands against unsanctioned infill by unplanned development. Urban planning activities

          will support the development and/or updating of structure plans, or master plans (i.e., General Planning Schemes,

          GPS). These activities will ensure that GPS are in alignment with the GoT's Five Year Development Plan (FYDP),

          and that they include capital investment prioritization, take into account local economic development needs, and

          include drainage and resilience needs. As part of this activity, the project will establish and train members of

          local advisory committees or working groups that will provide input into the planning tools developed and will

          engage citizens to consult on the design and operational arrangements of future investments;

      (c) Urban service delivery and operations and maintenance activities aim to promote integrated, coordinated, and

          preventative approach to the life-cycle management of key municipal facilities. Activities to be financed under the

          project will support structuring performance-based contracts with service providers in three key areas: (i)

          stormwater drainage maintenance ; (ii) solid waste management (SWM), particularly for centralized fee collection

          and landfill management; and (iii) municipal facilities (markets, lorry parks, bus terminals, minibus stands,

          abattoirs, open spaces, and streetlights). To address poor operations and maintenance (O&M) of municipal

          facilities, the activities will also focus on updating Standard Operating Procedures (SOP) and adopting them in

          formal contracts for O&M of the key municipal facilities. SWM-focused activities will support LGAs in refinement

          and/or development of licensing systems for waste collectors at the local level, in order to ensure better

          standardization and performance of contractor operations;







                                                                                                                   Page 14 of 54


         The World Bank

         Tanzania Cities Transforming Infrastructure and Competitiveness Project (P171189)







     (d) Mainstreaming urban resilience activities are aligned with the three pillars of the World Bank-executed activities

         under the Tanzania Urban Resilience Program (TURP): (i) risk identification; (ii) risk reduction; and (iii) disaster

         preparedness and emergency management. TA will support each LGA to develop a Community Resilience Plan,

         which will identify opportunities for engaging community groups in operations and maintenance, monitoring and

         reporting activities for improving resilience through the establishment of community resilience plans. These may

         include, for example, youth employment schemes for data collection on flood and waterlog-prone locations, illegal

         dumping sites, removal of waste or debris from drains, tree planting and growing and disaster risk reduction and

         environmental restoration. Other areas of focus may include disaster preparedness and emergency management

         activities, emergency needs assessment and response plans, emergency communications equipment,

         training/exercises/drills, emergency operations center support, damage assessment support through aerial

         surveys and mapping post floods, community response plans and early warning system pilots. The preparation

         and training as part of this activity would overlap with the urban planning activity ("b" above) to coordinate citizen

         consultation, information sharing, monitoring and grievance redress to local authorities;

     (e) Economic competitiveness activities aim to position cities to channel rapid urban growth into an enabling

         environment for economic development. Activities to be financed under the project will include (i) local economic

         development planning, such as economic cluster and value chain analysis and development strategies; (ii)

         development of special area plans (SAP) that identify prioritized investment areas for local economic development

         (i.e., industrial and commercial centers); and (iii) detailed planning schemes (DPS) for key commercial and

         industrial areas identified in SAPs, aiming to foster nascent sectors in areas of LGAs' competitive advantage. The

         priority areas such as industrial and commercial centers identified in SAPs can subsequently be regularized

         through the issuance of Certificates of Rights of Occupancy under the Land Tenure Improvement Project (LTIP).

         Capacity building as well as detailed program and capital works scoping for fostering nascent production-oriented

         sectors will support specialization and the GoT's industrialization goals.



24.     In addition to thematic institutional strengthening, Component 1 will also finance project preparation activities

that will support analytical, conceptual or similar work to identify, prioritize or provide design services for future

subprojects or catalytic projects.

title: Productive, Inclusive, and Resilient Urban Infrastructure (US$228 million equivalent)
text:
25.      This component finances interventions that promote urban productivity, inclusiveness, and climate resilience

in participating cities. LGAs have prepared multi-year capital investment plans, based on council and regional strategic

plans and master plans, and drawing from Local Economic Development Strategies and the Drainage and Sanitation

Development Plans (where those exist). Urban infrastructure investments under this Component have been prioritized by

PO-RALG and local government authorities based on the following criteria and principles: (a) population size and density;

(b) vulnerability to natural disasters; (c) income levels; and (d) lack of access to basic infrastructure and services.



26.       Participating LGAs are clustered into three Tiers based on population size, and investments will follow a phased

approach 31. Phase 1 of the project, covered under this proposed financing, will finance the preparation of all subprojects

for all cities in Tiers 1, 2 and 3. Implementation of subprojects will be split in two phases: a) implementation of subprojects





31Tiers are determined based on population and growth rate; Tier 1 cities have populations over 250,000 and annual growth rates of at least 1.5

percent, Tier 2 cities have populations below 250,000 and annual growth rates of less than 1.5 percent and Tier 3 cities are new LGAs that were

previously not included in TSCP or ULGSP.

in Tier 1 cities (largest cities) and selected Tier 2 cities 32 will be covered under Phase 1. Under Phase 2 there is possibility

to expand the scope of the project in the near future, possibly through an additional financing, to incorporate all

participating LGAs not currently eligible to receive funds for subproject implementation under Phase 1.



27.     Conceptual designs for Tier 1 cities, amounting to over US$168 million, have been prepared. Detailed subproject

designs are currently being finalized. Of the 54 subprojects being prepared for Tier 1 cities, three have submitted draft

site-specific ESIA and RAP documents which will be finalized by mid-June 2022. 33



28.      Project funds will target investments along the following key themes:

(a) Productivity investments will aim to strengthen rural-urban connectivity by supporting linkages between villages

    and secondary cities. Investments would include road, drainage and basic infrastructure upgrades inter alia with a

    focus in small-scale industrial areas, aiming to promote economic opportunities and job creation. Drawing from

    priorities indicated in local and regional strategic plans and master plans, LGAs in secondary and tertiary cities will

    prioritize capital investments in areas where clusters of economic activity exist (e.g. Zongomela Economic Cluster in

    Kahama,). Many of these clusters are not well serviced with basic infrastructure networks (e.g. roads and drainage).

    Coordination with water, electricity, and sanitation utilities will be facilitated and designs will incorporate low carbon,

    energy efficient principles. The focus on economic clusters builds on work done under the Dar es Salaam Urban Jobs

    Program (2018-21) 34, which supported the development of entrepreneurial skills in Tanzanian cities.

    Complementarities between skill development activities and urban infrastructure investments will be leveraged to

    provide better jobs and economic opportunities in beneficiary cities. The nature and location of investments financed

    by the project will be guided by the findings under the Local Economic Development Strategies completed for all

    Tanzania Strategic Cities Project (TSCP - P111153), as well as site-specific climate change vulnerability assessments.

(b) Inclusive investments will focus on upgrading selected low-income communities and will target vulnerable groups

    and women. This will be done through the improvement of basic services and strengthening local government

    authorities’ capacity in undertaking such upgrading works, including inter alia: (i) environmental-related works, such

    as storm water drainage, solid waste management (SWM), plastics management, energy efficient street lighting; and

    (ii) community related amenities, including green parks, markets, and bus stands. 35 Investments will be made in low-

    income communities or sub-wards. Upgrading of these community facilities will be done through community

    participatory approaches, including socio-economic surveys and focus group discussions aimed at soliciting beneficiary

    feedback to engage citizens not only in the planning but also in the implementation and monitoring of prioritized

    works. The project will use the latest data available from the 2018 Household Budget Survey to identify priority areas

    in participating LGAs, targeting: (i) dense, highly populated, and low-income areas with poor infrastructure; (ii)

    opportunities to connect to the primary road and drainage network as identified in completed master plans, general

    planning schemes, and strategic council plans; (iii) investments that discourage sprawl and encourage densification;

    and (iv) good practices from gender analysis to ensure that urban infrastructure designs are responsive to the needs

    of women.

(c) Resilience investments will build on outputs of TA completed under Component 1, and will finance investments in

    urban adaptation and resilience, focusing on flooding, earthquakes, drought risk and sea level rise. This will include

 Component 3 – Project Management (US$15 million equivalent)

29.     This component will finance inter alia the operational costs of the Project Coordination Team (PCT) to support

coordination, financial management, procurement, monitoring and evaluation, and environmental and social

management, to ensure the project is implemented efficiently, and in accordance with the fiduciary and environmental

and social requirements. The component will also finance the development and maintenance of a web-based remote

supervision tool, currently piloted under TURP and integrated to the Grievance Redress Mechanism (GRM), to monitor

how different project activities are implemented in each city, including physical and financial execution, compliance with

the World Bank’s Environmental and Social Framework (ESF), and beneficiary feedback. The component will also finance

the costs of communication, including the project website and social platform to support the project’s access to

information and citizen engagement.



 Component 4 – Contingent Emergency Response, CERC (US$0 million)



 30.     This component enables rapid response to eligible emergencies and disasters caused by natural and man-made

 events by providing contingent financing. Many TACTIC cities face increasing disaster risks associated with climate change

 impacts and rapid unplanned urbanization, with flooding during the rainy seasons being the most common recurring

 disaster. Several cities are in seismically active zones. This component will allow the GoT to access project funds to

 support immediate disaster response, rehabilitation, and reconstruction needs. The CERC will initially have no funding

 allocation, but upon its activation uncommitted funds from other project components will be reallocated to serve the

 eligible needs. Activation of the CERC will require the World Bank’s no-objection upon (a) declaration of an emergency

 by GoT , (b) submission of a request for support to the World Bank, and (c) preparation of an acceptable Emergency

 Action Plan by the GoT. PO-RALG will prepare a CERC Operations Manual to guide its activation and implementation

 arrangements which will be approved by the World Bank.

 by supporting urban local governments in Tanzania to contribute to all four key pillars: saving lives, protecting poor

 and vulnerable people, ensuring job creation, and strengthening policies, institutions, and investments for rebuilding

 32.     Gender Issues. The FY18-FY22 Tanzania CPF notes that gender disparities are still prevalent, cutting into

 women’s well-being, earnings, voice and agency. The Tanzania Gender Assessment finds that women have lower levels

 of agency, which is reflected in decision making power. Women participate in very few decisions related to their health

 or household purchases. Tanzania ranked 67 out of 153 countries in 2020 in the Global Gender Gap Report of the World

 Economic Forum; in terms of economic participation and opportunity, its rank was 63, with several indicators revealing

 continuing gaps between men and women. Women face harassment and violence in public spaces and while using public

 transportation; a survey of female commuters in Dar es Salaam found 58 percent experienced some form of gender-

 based violence at least one time in the past six months. 39,40 Women represented only 31 percent of the participants in

 select consultations under a previous urban project for an affected area that was composed of nearly 50 percent female-

 headed households. Increasing the participation and decision-making role of women in urban planning can improve the

 quality and inclusiveness of infrastructure investments. 41

 7.      This subcomponent will support integrated landscape planning in 13 sub-basins (Table 2.1.) to

 improve the management of natural resources and land use, including for enhanced food security. The

 subcomponent will include the following activities: (a) supporting subnational 62 multi-stakeholder

 coordination platforms on land-use planning by bringing in the existing Basin Management Board of the

 various basins where the project is operating; (b) developing spatial planning tools; and (c) developing

 and facilitating integrated land-use plans. The development of these plans is critical for ensuring that land

 resources are used and managed in a way that enhances absorptive and adaptive capacity to climate

 change, promoting resilience broadly at the landscape level.

 8.       It will also support the development of spatial planning tools for mapping analysis and monitoring

 impacts. These tools could include Forest, Cocoa and ASM Monitoring Systems,63 tree

 registration/counting/carbon accounting system, relevant databases and maps, participatory mapping

 tools, and so on. The objective of developing these tools is to help inform decision-makers on what is

 happening in the landscape so that they can make more effective decisions on planning and monitor the

title: Airborne geo-physics and geological surveys (US$6.58 million, all IDA)
text:
11.      As part of the Government’s effort to improve the understanding of the national geology and

 subsoil resources, this subcomponent will support geological investigations to analyze geomorphological

 trends, mineral occurrences, and interlinkages between different land and resources uses. These

 investigations will inform the trade-offs between competing land uses as well as the feasibility of land

 restoration. Moreover, investigations will also identify economically viable mineral reservation areas for

 small-scale miners. Currently, about 150 areas covering 5,400 km2 have been designated for ASM.

 However, there is the need to conduct a detailed investigation to ensure the areas are viable and that

 environmental impacts are manageable before licensing to prospective applicants. Currently, only nine of

 these areas have been explored, and those that proved positive were demarcated to small-scale miners.

 A minimum of 1,000 km2 of land will be prospected geologically over the period of the project. This activity

 would be a key criterion for reducing the degradation of land by informal miners and thus contributing to

 climate change mitigation potential of the project. Identification and allocation of lands suitable for SSM
