 13.     The objective of this activity is to support the design and rollout of a robust mining operations’

 monitoring and inspection system. It will consist of three sub-objectives: (a) assess and develop the

 regulatory framework and guidelines governing E&S compliance and control mechanisms; (b) develop

 standard report templates and support selective inspections of ASM operations in accordance with

 regulations; and (c) establish mechanisms and tools for monitoring ASM operations through a database

 management system which will facilitate standardized and systematic control and reporting of operations.



 14.      The activity will also provide capacity building to officers in the FC, the EPA, and the MC in the

 monitoring and management of E&S impacts from ASM. These topics will include (a) water management;

 (b) management of hazardous products and waste; (c) community consultation; (d) health and safety; and

 (e) mine rehabilitation. The activity will strengthen institutional partnerships, coordination, and data

 development around ASM's forest impacts and encourage forest protection and restoration, particularly

 at the licensing and decommissioning stages.



 15.     The subcomponent will also support community outreach, public education, and awareness

 creation on the revised ASM regulatory framework to foster understanding and full compliance with

 sector guidelines. Activities will also aim to promote broad stakeholder consultations in the drafting of

 legal and regulatory instruments required for ASM formalization and modernization. To complement the

 development of strong environmental impact legislation, policy dialogues will also engage stakeholders





                                                                                                   Page 100 of 143


The World Bank

Ghana Landscape Restoration and Small-Scale Mining Project (P171933)







 on community-centered forest risk mitigation incentives. This will help strengthen resource and

 environmental governance in the ASM sector.



 16.      The subcomponent will finance modernization of the licensing system to allow registration of SSM

 license holders as well as inclusion of a new medium-scale license category. An important objective under

 this subcomponent will be to facilitate women’s access to mineral licenses to promote female

 entrepreneurship in ASM, as restrictions in access to land for mining have been raised as a specific concern

 during project consultations. To achieve this, technical solutions must be developed to enable

 decentralized registration at the regional and district offices. This will require the acquisition of both

 software and hardware as well as training of MC officials and the DMCs. One objective will be to promote

 female entrepreneurship and facilitate women’s access to mineral licenses. The project activities to

 register informal miners will also designate mining activities within specific land areas. This formalization

 will contribute to better enforcement of protected forest arears and enhanced riverbank protection as

 well as mitigate forest degradation. The FC and EPA will be equipped with digital monitoring and reporting

 systems. Regulation and training on water and effluent discharge management will enhance adaptive

 capacity of ecosystems and communities.



 17.     As part of the efforts to strengthen sector formalization, this subcomponent will finance

 stakeholder dialogues on mainstreaming ASM into the EITI framework, as a follow-up to work undertaken

 in the preliminary Scoping Study on the Incorporation of ASM in Ghana EITI (2015). The activity will lay

 the groundwork for the design of a mainstreaming road map and implementation strategy at the national

 and subnational level. Key areas of collaboration will include developing ASM reporting guidelines and

 templates, tightening public disclosure requirements under the Minerals and Mining Act, and

 strengthening accessibility of ASM data through upgrades to the mining cadaster.



 18.      Outputs will include revised legal and regulatory instruments to reflect the changing nature of the

 ASM industry in Ghana. It is also anticipated to develop a modernized mineral cadaster system to register

 all types of mineral licenses from small-scale to large-scale operators, including geographic information

 system-based software to project and locate license holders.

title: Training and technology transfer (US$5.68 million, all IDA).
text:
19.      The objective of this subcomponent is to build local-level capacity in sustainable ASM techniques

 and sector oversight management. This will incorporate capacity-building support to ASM operators as

 well as district mining officers of the MC, EPA district officers, and members of the DSMCs to enable them

 to discharge their duties effectively and efficiently. Training of ASM operators will include aspects of

 climate-smart and forest-smart mining, such as reduction and management of mine waste, reduced

 clearance of vegetation, post-mining restoration of degraded land, and capacity building of the small-scale

 miners on natural/climate risk and disaster response. This is expected to also mitigate erosion and

 improve streamflow management around abandoned mine sites. Resulting revegetation will also have

 climate mitigation benefits. The project will prioritize skills development and support to women, the

 youth, and other vulnerable groups. This will help them start and operate businesses that create value

 along and outside of the ASM value chain.



 20.     The subcomponent will aim to promote sustainable and well-managed ASM operations, focusing

 on improved operational procedures and practical application of global best practices. The subcomponent

 will support establishing an ASM business support center (Incubation Center) to provide advisory, training,



                                                                                                     Page 101 of 143


The World Bank

Ghana Landscape Restoration and Small-Scale Mining Project (P171933)







 and technical services for ASM business as well as the establishment of a pilot center of excellence (Mining

 Demonstration Center) demonstrating best practice ASM processes. The scope of services envisaged

 under this subcomponent will include (a) mercury-free processing; (b) training on enterprise skills and

 forming business entities; (c) regulatory compliance; (d) environmental management and mine

 rehabilitation; (e) technology transfer; (f) health and safety; and (g) social responsibility. The

 Demonstration Center will facilitate continuous capacity building for ASM operators, mining engineers,

 and extension service agents, among others. Activities through the Demonstration Center will prioritize

 the practical demonstration of sustainable and environmentally friendly mining practices (managed in a

 way that minimizes the environmental and climate footprint) such as mercury-free gold extraction and

 the adoption of safe and appropriate local technologies. The subcomponent will additionally include

 limited production and deployment of improved and affordable mercury retorts (colloquially called Sika

 Bukyia) in ASM gold extraction and processing for improved gold recovery.

title: Traceability of ASM production and value addition (US$2.88 million, all IDA)
text:
21.      This subcomponent will aim to establish multi-stakeholder partnerships to strengthen ASM supply

 chains and improve market access to ASMs for greater value creation. The project will also invest in

 strengthening traceability of ASM output as a means to increase profit retention and enhance benefit-

 sharing of the value created. The PMMC will acquire additional assaying equipment to meet the expected

 increase in demand for testing and assaying. This equipment will encompass X-ray machines for analysis

 of the mineral composition as well as fire assay equipment, precision scales, and associated software. It

 is also envisioned that software applications will be developed for online tracking of sales and transfers

 between registered miners, traders, and buying centers to trace products from source of origin to end

 destination.



 22.      An elaborate outreach and training campaign will be supported to inform and educate ASM

 operators about the trading patterns and registration procedures for producers and merchants. It is also

 envisioned that clusters and cooperatives of miners will be developed; these will require training to

 simplify ASM operators’ access to the trading networks. The activity will improve awareness of the forest

 impacts associated with ASM supply chains and support strategies to minimize forest risks in ASM

 production, supply chain, and market standards and mechanisms. The project will reduce the demand for

 fuelwood because it will incentivize artisanal and small-scale miners to switch amalgamation and mineral

 processing to formal processing centers which are more energy efficient. This will replace home-based

 amalgamation using fuelwood to more efficient technology used by the PMMC.

 community needs but will fall under the following categories: (a) silvo-pastoral activities will support

 33.      This subcomponent will support the provision of small post-harvest structures, improve market

 access, and promote value addition of selected cash crop commodities (cocoa [in the Transition zone] and

 cashew and shea [in the savannah zone]) which have been identified as priority commodities for the

 project; other commodities may be identified and added later on. The objective of this activity is to

 provide farmers with the necessary quality and leverage to compete in markets and further improve their

 livelihoods. This activity will aim to improve marketability and quality of the products through the

 provision of training that is tailored to existing supply chains and market buyers. In addition, to help

 professionalize farmer associations, the project will support the conversion of associations into formal

 cooperatives to improve their access to larger markets, where possible, mostly for cocoa and cashew. In

 this context, the activities will be conducted through COCOBOD and its association with the CFI.

 Improvements in value chains will have both climate change mitigation and adaptation benefits, as the

 production systems will be adapted to changing climatic conditions while improvements in processing will

 reduce wastage of natural resources.



 34.      It will also promote gender-inclusive alternative livelihoods by investing in the implementation of

 natural resources-based livelihoods activities to reduce pressures on the forests and to create income-

 earning opportunities besides the farming activities, with a specific focus on supporting women’s

 groups/associations to ensure women’s equal participation in economic activities and access to markets.

 The project support will ensure that products readily available to the communities can be used for value

 addition, such as baobab leaves’ processing, beekeeping, soap making, dairy processing, snail rearing,

 poultry and rabbit rearing, groundnut processing (oil and paste production), production of bamboo

 handicrafts, and so on, to enhance community livelihoods and food security. The project will provide

 inputs required for activities (such as processing equipment) and required technical assistance and

 training, to ensure adequate quality for market access. The project support will give special consideration

 to gender-sensitive issues that could impede women’s abilities to participate effectively in economic

 activities and devise ways to overcome these issues.



 35.     In addition, up to 50 communities will be trained on and supported in the establishment of VSLAs.

 The groups will be trained on the basics of FM, such as bookkeeping, and will be provided with VSLA

 savings boxes and other required equipment.



 36.     This subcomponent will also support the provision of performance-based payments to farmers

 electing to participate in the scheme through establishing tree cover in the catchment areas. Because of

 limited agricultural revenue during the tree maturity period and a lack of access to seedlings, farmers are

 unable to easily transition into tree farming. As part of the inputs (Subcomponent 3.1), the project will

 provide mango and other tree seedlings of importance to farmers to augment their current land uses:

 agricultural production of maize, groundnut, and rice. Contingent on 75 percent of trees surviving after

 one year (based on field verification), the project will pay performance-based cash incentives to

 participating farmers. This approach was already piloted under the SLWMP and has proven to be a

 prevention of forest loss due to mining. Activities will include mapping, prioritization, and characterization

 clean-up approaches and techniques, which will inform site-specific rehabilitation plans. Monitoring of

 44.       Under this subcomponent, the project will also set up demonstration sites of appropriate

 rehabilitation approaches for a small number of selected abandoned mine sites as part of the ILM plans

 and FMPs, with a total area of approximately 2,000 ha. These activities will be closely coordinated with

 parallel activities under the FIP. The objective of the activity would be to create awareness of

 rehabilitation and economic potentials of abandoned mine sites among relevant stakeholders and

title: Competitive Reinforcement Initiatives (US$8 million equivalent)
text:
37.      This subcomponent will finance CRIs for export-oriented agricultural and manufacturing

   clusters.23 A CRI is a highly structured process that intertwines industry analysis with sector-specific public-

   private dialogue (PPD) and may include capacity building when forming a team to undertake the CRIs. The

   project has started setting up a team of competitiveness specialists to carry out the CRIs. The

   competitiveness specialists will be supervised by the PCU, supported by an international consulting firm,

   and will be mostly based in the regions. In the CRI process, the industry analysis (a) identifies how

   participating private sector firms/farms can compete in more attractive markets, in particular which new

   skills and activities are needed to compete; (b) is market oriented and provides timely market intelligence

   which can inform investment decisions; and (c) aims to find solutions that are the least distortive as

   possible (for example, avoiding long-term subsidies and monopsonies). Furthermore, it identifies the

   potential market failures that constrain the private sector’s competitiveness and evolution and corollary

   government reforms required to overcome them. The PPD process motivates value chain actors to be

   agents of change within the value chain. Building capacity of the Government to undertake CRIs ensures

   ownership of its competitiveness agenda. The project will use a sequential approach whereby the CRIs

   will inform the investments, reforms, and activities to be financed under Components 1, 2, and 3. A

   detailed description of the CRI process and implementation in the CVJET Project is presented in Annex 4.



   38.     To contribute to more and better jobs in the supported value chains, the project will integrate

   survey techniques to measure job creation and job quality for the supported value chains. The CRI

   methodology lends itself well to a ‘Jobs in Value Chains Analytical Process’24 given that the CRI approach

   already includes elements such as value chain mapping, firm and smallholder interviews, PPD, and value

   chain analysis. The competitiveness specialists’ presence in the field will support the collection of baseline

   data for the value chains and its beneficiaries. This effort will be supported by the M&E specialist in the

   PCU and possibly a survey firm to adapt the survey questionnaires and sampling approach to the project.



   39.      The project will undertake up to 10 CRIs over the life of the project, starting with mango,

   plastics, rubber, pineapple, and palm oil. The project will also undertake CRIs for cocoa and cashew but

   will not finance investments for these two value chains as CRI recommendations will be shared with the

   ongoing and planned International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD)- and IDA-funded

   programs focused on developing the cashew and cocoa GVCs for potential investments.25 The

   identification of the initial CRIs is based on the priority sectors identified in the CPSD, the Manufacturing

   Sector Scan26, and the Government’s Vision 2030 Strategic Plan. The CPSD identified five sectors with high

   potential for growth—cashew, rubber, cotton, palm oil, and horticulture (mango, pineapple, and

   banana)—based on five criteria: (a) revealed comparative advantage; (b) evolution of global demand; (c)

   43.      This subcomponent aims to enhance the competitiveness of Ivorian farmers and enterprises in

   supported value chains by financing investment mechanisms that will provide common services and

   productive assets currently missing but needed to increase quality standards, add value to products,

   and access higher value-added markets. Operationalizing GVCs requires an integral and comprehensive

   approach that addresses all market failures along the value chain. The supported value chains face market

   failures such as coordination failures (primarily), information asymmetries, underdevelopment of public

   goods (including club goods), and negative externalities. The CRIs will identify the market failures affecting

   the supported value chains and propose the policy reforms and common services required to overcome

   them. Most commonly, these services would be club goods28 that require economies of scale. The

   investments in this component will be aligned with the following principles: (a) follow a Maximizing

   Finance for Development (MFD) approach: when feasible, the common services will be delivered by the

   private sector and (b) create the least market distortions (for example, long-term subsidies, monopsonies,

   and so on). An example of some coordination failures in the mango value chain are presented in Box 2.



   44.     This subcomponent will finance two investment mechanisms and digital solutions. The

   investment mechanisms are (a) Matching Grants for Common Services and (b) Provision or construction

   of Common Productive Assets, with Matching Grants. In this operation, common services and common

   productive assets differ based on whether service providers are currently able to provide the services

   proposed by the CRIs or not. The Matching Grants for Common Services are for common services where

   service providers already exist in the market. Mechanism 2 is designed to provide (that is, construct, buy)

   new, common productive assets for which there are no private operators capable of providing the service

   due to high upfront costs of setting up the assets or services. The investment mechanisms will use digital

   solutions (for example, blockchain) for all supported value chains, for traceability, quality control, and

   accounting purposes. Some value chains may require the use of both investment mechanisms.









   28 Club goods are a sub-type of public goods that are excludable but non-rivalrous—that is, it is not diminished as access is

   broadened, but users can be prevented from accessing it. Classic examples of club goods are cinemas, private parks, or satellite

   television. In the context of industrial development, club goods are often underprovided. This happens for two reasons: (a) it is

   difficult to enforce the exclusion of non-payers (and hence the club good becomes a public good, with problems of ‘free riding’)

   or (b) individuals cannot coordinate among themselves to finance the provision of the club good or club service.

     Box 2. Examples of Coordination Market Failures in the Mango Value Chain and Early Results for Piloting

     Value Chain Blockchain Solution in Haiti

     With an annual production of around 150,000 tons, of which 32,000 tons are exported per year, Côte d'Ivoire is

     the leading exporter of mangoes in Africa and the second supplier to the European market. Mango is the third

     most exported fruit from Côte d'Ivoire, after banana and pineapple. The primary mango season extends from

     January through May and the mango sector includes approximately 7,000 actors. The main stakeholders are (a)

     producers; (b) exporters with their own conditioning facilities; (c) processors; (d) private companies (input

     suppliers, box suppliers, post-harvest infrastructure, and loading operation at the fruit terminal at the port); and

     (e) research centers. Available data reveal that a case of mangoes (30 mangoes) sold for CFAF 1,478 (US$2.71) in

     2012 and CFAF 1,012 (US$1.86)—or US$0.06 cents per mango—in 2013, at farmgate. Farmers’ revenues

     fluctuated around CFAF 130,950 (US$240) between the 2011 and 2013 seasons.

     Mangoes in the European market sell for approximately US$2 per kg (approximately US$2 for two mangoes). To

     increase farmers’ revenues, a series of coordination failures need to be addressed to sell directly to the European

     market. For example, mangoes need hot-water treatment to control for fruit fly larvae, their temperature needs

     to be quickly lowered to around 12°C and they require temperature-controlled logistics within a few hours after

     treatment to ensure longer shelf life until destination, where the mangoes can ripen. Despite the presence of

     logistic services in Côte d’Ivoire, the mango farmers are not organized nor have access to the financing required

     to coordinate the value chain services to access these export market. On the financing side, the farmers require

     supply chain financing rather than other types of loans. In particular, they need short-term advances that use the

     product—that is, the mangoes kept under strict quality control—as the collateral.

     A public blockchain solution for value chains was recently piloted in the Haiti Business Development and

     Investment Project (P123974). To increase the incomes of fresh fruit producers, especially mango farmers, the

     project connected producers in Haiti to consumers in the North American market. Beyond enabling the sale of

     mangoes in the international market, the project has supported the training of producers in proper harvesting

     techniques, and transport and cold chain management, which can optimize post-harvest yields. The project set

     up a cold chain logistics service in key producing regions of the country to sell fresh fruit to the United States and

     strengthen the competitiveness of Haiti’s fresh fruit sector. Connecting producers to this key market has t he

     potential to raise them out of poverty and increase overall economic resilience. As a result of the project’s CRIs,

     use of the blockchain solution and provision of third-party temperature-controlled logistics providers, in 2020, 58

     mango farmers involved in the project exported directly, without intermediaries, nearly 52,000 pounds of

     mangoes to the United States. These sales generated over 238 percent higher income than if these mangoes were

     sold on the local market. The project closes in 2021 and has also expanded to specialty coffee, fine cacao, and

     avocado to the United States using the same system.

   1.2.1: Investment Mechanism 1 - Matching Grants for Common Services (US$30 million equivalent)



   45.      The economic rationale of these Matching Grants is to support eligible beneficiaries (farmers

   and firms) to meet new quality standards, primarily for the EU or US markets, through common services

   required to compete in more attractive markets. In particular, these Matching Grants are designed to

   correct coordination failures faced by farmers and firms in supported value chains by providing the

   common services that are currently missing (and for which service providers already exist in the market

   but are not providing the service to a particular area or group due to coordination failures). Under this

   mechanism, the PCU would competitively select service providers based on studies, technical

   specifications, or SOPs developed under Subcomponent 1.1.



   46.     The Matching Grants for Common Services are an innovative instrument which would finance

   advance payments of eligible expenses. Examples of eligible expenses include the following types of

   services: postharvest temperature-controlled or other specialized logistics service, collection points,

   brokerage services, packaging facilities, harvest planning or maturity mapping services29, international

   shipping/export, technical assistance and training (for example, dissemination of quality certification and

   standardization initiatives and middle management training), and/or a combination of these services. To

   address coordination failure(s), advances are needed to make the service available to the cluster actors;

   however, to control for the risk of abuse of advance payment of eligible expenses, a set of eligibility

   conditions must be met to activate the mechanism. These include (a) pre-registration of beneficiaries; (b)

   meeting of quality standards defined by SOPs or other specifications and ensuring quality control provided

   by a third-party service provider; (c) use of the blockchain solution by the service provider to schedule

   pickups, ensure quality control, consolidate small lots into larger batches for export, and so on; and (d)

   use of an escrow account to manage advances and payments based on instructions received from the

   blockchain solution.30



   47.     By combining the matching grant advances with the eligibility conditions above, the funds will

   be replenished into an escrow account to be reinvested in more common services in the supported

   value chains. The key principle of any of the supported export initiatives is that the products will be

   competitive and will not need any subsidy to cover any of the extra costs involved. However, the Matching

   Grant mechanism needs to provide funds to allow the farmers and service providers to engage and export.

   Once the products are exported, sold, and the profits received, the beneficiaries will be ready to save for

   future reinvestment of the subsidy received as a Matching Grant. To reinforce future reinvestments, the

   PCU will open a Joint Savings Account for the beneficiaries which would allow the beneficiaries to finance

   future common services. Eligible common services for investment by the beneficiaries would include any

   common service that would support production, harvest, or post-harvest activities of the cluster. The

   modalities and rules relative to the Joint Savings Account will be further defined in the Matching Grants

   Manual. In total, it is expected that the Matching Grants for Common Services will support an estimated

   3,000 farmers and 100 firms and allow for an average value of advances of US$7,000 per beneficiary.

   50.      While this mechanism would provide new opportunities for the beneficiaries to export directly

   to markets, it also implies more risk for them. The beneficiaries are becoming exporters that assume the

   rewards of avoiding commercial intermediaries but also the entrepreneurial risks associated. The three

   most significant risks are (a) economies of scale: if the common service does not reach minimum efficient

   scale, the fixed costs of exports can result in lower margins or even losses; (b) market shocks: the producer

   directly faces all destination market shocks; even if destination markets can be targeted based on average

   spot market prices for certain periods, any price shocks, up or down, will be absorbed by the beneficiaries

   now; and (c) supply constraints for growth: If the producers are successful in increasing value through

   exports and want to increase production, they may face input shortages that the local market dynamic

   may take time to supply. This is why during the CRI, the teams will need to present scenarios to the

   beneficiaries with high price, low price, unsuccessful sale, and breakeven, to evaluate every potential

   product. The key is always the premium between local price and price at destination, which is a variable

   due to existing competition during the different production windows and demand. Key assumptions and

   potential risks associated with this mechanism are further discussed in Annex 4.



   51.     All of the product tracking and calculations will be done on the blockchain solution platform.

   The service provider will be responsible for using the blockchain solution to enter the necessary data and

   information. Midway through the project, the Government will explore the feasibility of scaling up the

   investment mechanism (including the SOPs, third-party quality control, and a blockchain solution for

   tracking goods and financial flows) in the private sector through a financial institution, with a view to

   offering supply chain financing to small farmers and firms.

   1.2.2: Investment Mechanism 2 - Provision or construction of Common Productive Assets (US$28 million

   equivalent)



   52.      This mechanism will finance common productive assets in cases where significant physical

   assets are needed and there are no private operators able to provide the assets or service due to high

   upfront investments in infrastructure or goods. In these circumstances, private sector participation is

   difficult or limited. Examples of these types of assets include specialized equipment and technology

   related to post-harvest handling and cold chain logistics (for example, mobile packing units); pilot

   production and product testing facilities (for example, optimize the setup of the machines, molds, or the

   product before final industrialization); rapid prototyping; physical laboratory testing; and specialized

   equipment and machinery required to meeting international standards and specialized training. This

   investment mechanism will also use a digital solution (for example, blockchain) to support traceability and

   accounting.



   53.     Mobile packing units would allow farmers to overcome ‘first mile’ constraints, in particular

   where the handling time between harvest and cooling is needed to preserve the quality of temperature-

   sensitive products, such as fruits. Mobile packing units would be designed through the post-CRI studies

   (Subcomponent 1.2). The firm responsible for the design of the unit would need to ensure compliance

   with phytosanitary, quarantine, or customs clearance or inspection requirements by authorities for fresh

   exported products (whether national or that of the destination country).



   54.      The Pilot Production and Product Testing Facilities (PPPTFs) would provide services that require

   specialized equipment and know-how not available in the local market. Among the possible services to

   be offered by the PPPTFs are prototyping and realization of pilots, tests and certification, specialized

   training, and production of short series. For prototyping and piloting, the aim is to support the

   beneficiaries (firms in supported clusters) to develop and test innovative, replicable, scalable, and

   financially viable models of future products. Testing and certification will require equipment,

   technological infrastructure, and laboratories to support firms in their technological development

   processes, test and certification of materials, devices, products, and processes.



   55.      The CRIs undertaken before PPPTF development will allow the project to ensure that the PPPTFs

   will correct market failures and will not be “white elephants”. Given the importance of quality upgrading

   for both the agri-business and manufacturing sectors for sectoral transformation, the project will support

   up to three PPPTFs. The design and governance of each PPPTF will differ according to the level of

   development of the supported clusters. Depending on the design of PPPTF required, the project may

   finance the works to build the facilities, the procurement of equipment, and the recruitment of managers,

   technicians, or trainers. However, renting a location to house the PPPTF is also a viable option. The PPPTFs

   will be built or set up in rented facilities on public land, through long term leases. It is estimated that each

   PPPTF would require approximately 2000m2 – 10,000 m2. In cases where construction of the PPPTF is

   required, the land would be acquired through the leasing of public industrial lands (i.e. Industrial Zone or

   Free Zone). The amount to be paid under the lease is established by Decree and is not subject to market

   fluctuations or distortions. The project would finance the usage fees for long-term leases as set forth in

   Decree No. 2015-810 (December 2015), or any future decrees that establish fees for industrial land. These

   land expenditures have been authorized exceptionally by the Regional Vice President.

   56.       In Côte d’Ivoire, clusters are primarily embryonic or developing. Common services for embryonic

   clusters tend to focus on testing and training. Common services for developing or more developed clusters

   require more significant product/machinery testing and technological solutions for greater productive

   flexibility, shorter design time, shorter industrialization time, and greater ability to adapt to changes and

   customization of orders (rapid prototyping, rapid manufacturing, and high-speed manufacturing). Under

   the project, two types of governance models of the PPPTF are possible: (a) government owned with a

   concession for a private operator to manage and operate the facility and (b) transfer to the private sector

   (that is, cluster actors).



   Matching Grants for Common Productive Assets (US$13 million equivalent)



   57.      This Matching Grant mechanism will support eligible beneficiaries to access and use common

   productive assets financed under Mechanism 2. The Matching Grants for the Common Productive Assets

   comprise two windows. The beneficiaries of the Matching Grants will be eligible farmers and/or firms

   participating along the supported value chains. The Matching Grants Manual will define the eligibility

   criteria and matching levels based on actual income and /or number of employees. Window A will allow

   for access and use of Government-owned common productive assets. It is estimated that the Matching

   Grant will benefit approximately 1,500 farmers and 80 firms for an average amount of US$2,000 each

   (cumulative because the farmers and firms would likely use the common productive assets multiple

   times). Window B will allow for the transfer of the Government-owned common productive assets to the

   cluster members (or private sector). For Window B, the Matching Grant will also allow for subsidizing the

   purchase of ‘shares’ of the common productive assets by the cluster members, relative to their usage of

   the common productive assets (which will be recorded in the blockchain system). These are exclusively

   assets that have been procured through the project. It is estimated that the matching grant will benefit

   approximately 500 farmers and 50 firms. If the beneficiaries are matched for buying shares at the salvage

   value of the common productive asset, Matching Grant amounts of approximately US$10,000 each are

   expected. The Matching Grant Manual will be a disbursement condition.



   1.2.3: Digital solutions for supported value chains (US$1 million equivalent)



   58.     All of the value chains supported by the project will use a digital solution (for example,

   Distributed Ledger Technology [DLT] or blockchain) to track products, carbon credits, and financial flows

   along the value chain. Subcomponent 1.2.3 will finance the development and hosting of such a digital

   platform for tracking products, carbon credits, and financing flows in supported value chains. A blockchain

   platform would allow the supply chain to be digitized, by creating ‘smart contracts’ between all the actors

   along the value chain and tracking the products and payments. Furthermore, the blockchain will allow the

   service provider to consolidate smaller lots into larger batches for export and to be able to trace each lot

   back to the producer. For example, a logistics service provider could create automatic smart contracts in

   a blockchain system for each shipment. An advantage of a blockchain system is that the data would not

   be owned by one company but by the farmer or MSME as it will be hosted on a public blockchain platform.

   A blockchain system would also bring transparency to the value chain. The farmer would also gain more

   revenue (due to the disappearance of non-value-adding intermediaries, as well as more market power).

   Such digital solutions can be further scaled up beyond the value chains supported through this project

   once the technology is available and has proven to be effective in the Ivorian context.

   59.      The digital solutions would be customized and piloted for each value chain that requires it. The

   digital solution(s) would connect all parties in the value chain and be used by the service provider, the

   identity manager, and the financial intermediaries. This activity would establish the proof of concept for

   supply chain financing along value chains using the product as collateral. This activity would be

   implemented in connection with Investment Mechanism 1: Matching Grants for Common Services, which

   would provide the working capital funds to be held in escrow and replenished with payment by buyers.

   The primary users of the digital solution(s) will notably be the identity manager, the service provider, and

   the partner financial institution. The identity manager is responsible for collecting and storing all the data

   in the digital system, including farmers or firms’ data.



   60.     The blockchain solution will also allow for the tokenization of carbon credits by project

   beneficiaries. This would allow the project beneficiaries to also participate in the carbon credit market by

   monetizing and tokenizing their natural resources through the blockchain solution. These carbon credits

   can then be traded and used as a carbon offset.

title: Support to women in value chains (US$3 million equivalent)

61.      In an effort to promote gender equality and reduce gender gaps along the supported value

   chains, the project will support two interventions focused on increasing women’s labor force

   participation and promoting women’s entrepreneurship. The objective is to improve the quantity and

   quality of the women’s labor in the geographical areas of the supported value chains. These interventions

   are (a) the provision of childcare services, including mobile childcare services, to alleviate time constraints

   of women to increase their labor force participation and (b) personal initiative training, which focuses on

   developing non-cognitive skills and successful entrepreneurial behavior and has been demonstrated to be

   an effective psychology-based training for entrepreneurs, particularly women.



   1.3.1: Childcare services (US$2 million equivalent)



   62.     This intervention will provide childcare services to women in the geographical areas of the

   supported value chains with the objective of alleviating time constraints of women to increase their

   labor force participation. Based on ongoing Africa Gender Innovation Lab (GIL) research in Burkina Faso,

   the Democratic Republic of Congo, and Ethiopia, the childcare services could either be mobile crèches or

   community-based centers to ease the burden of care constraints and increase women’s labor supply. A

   diagnostic on the demand and supply for childcare in Côte d’Ivoire, financed by the Early Learning

   Partnership Multi-Donor Trust Fund of the World Bank, shows that in urban areas, women are willing to

   pay for childcare services but there is a lack of supply. In rural areas, childcare is primarily provided by

   family members.



   63.       The Burkina Faso Youth Employment and Skills Project (P130735) developed mobile creches to

   encourage women’s participation in a public works program, while also allowing young mothers to have

   their children nearby. Another alternative is community-based centers, as implemented in the GIL-led

   childcare pilots in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and Ethiopia. The DRC model uses a hybrid

   model between an informal system, in which groups of women are joined together and take turns as

   caretaker and a formal system, in which a school or classroom is financed by the project, and children are

   provided with food, toys, and activities. In the hybrid model, only infrastructure already existing in the

   village is used, and low-cost play-based curricula are used to promote child development.

Competitive Value Chains for Jobs and Economic Transformation Project (P172425)







   64.      To target the beneficiaries for this activity, the project will use data collected during the CRIs. The

   data collected will include geo-localization of the value chain actors, their gender, and if they have

   children, their age. This data will serve as the basis for targeting specific areas or villages with the highest

   concentration of women, to ensure the highest potential impact. Then, the PCU will hire a consultant to

   review infrastructure already existing in the selected areas or villages to see if that can be used.

   Expenditures may include monthly payments to creches, salaries for teachers or monitors, fuel, and

   communication for monthly education and health monitoring visits, and meals for children for mobile

   crèches. Eligible expenses will include operational expenses, consultant services, non-consultant services,

   goods, and food expenditures. Food expenditures, up to US$250,000, will be financed by IDA through this

   project, as per approval by the Regional Vice President. For similar projects, expenses were approximately

   US$833 per month per cheche. It is estimated that this project will finance no more than 12 cheches for

   24 months. Hybrid community-based centers also offer a low-cost option as it uses the existing

   infrastructure.



   65.     This component will be executed by childcare service providers, meaning a non-governmental

   organization (NGO) to be selected on a competitive basis by the Recipient to assist with the technical

   implementation of this component.



   1.3.2: Personal Initiative Training (US$1 million equivalent)



   66.      The CVJET Project will support women in the geographical areas of the supported value chains

   with an innovative training program such as personal initiative training that applies lessons from

   psychology to encourage women to act with an entrepreneurial mindset, with additional modules for

   increasing literacy levels. Standard business training programs aim to boost the incomes of self-employed

   business owners in developing countries, by teaching accounting, marketing, and other basic business

   skills. However, research shows limited impacts of this traditional business training approach.31 Through

   strengthening socio-emotional skills for female beneficiaries, the project aims to improve outcomes for

   women in the supported value chains. The training will include a couples training element, to garner intra-

   household support for the training. The outcomes may be observed in either the supported value chains

   or in non-supported value chains, in off-farm or alternative labor activities.

   69.     The objective of this subcomponent is to strengthen the institutional capacity of both the

   project is supporting value chains. It will be realized by the following:

                 on-site and off-site inspections, and so on;



           (b)   Supporting eligible MFIs’ capacities (including IT systems and equipment). Selection

                 criteria would be size of customer base, capacity-building needs, and location in rural or

                 remoted areas, where the project is supporting value chains.



   2.1.2: Strengthening digital financial infrastructure by financing a modern DCBS for eligible Microfinance

   Institutions (US$4.5 million equivalent)



   70.     The objective of this activity is to finance a key building block of the digital financial

   infrastructure to support eligible MFIs acquiring a DCBS, allowing them to expand into underserved

   areas by deploying a network of agents (instead of branches), launch digital financial services, and use

   modern reporting systems. The project will select MFIs using obsolete or inefficient management

The World Bank

Competitive Value Chains for Jobs and Economic Transformation Project (P172425)







   information system (MIS) but ready to or capable of making a technology leap. Selection criteria would

   be size of customers base, capacity-building needs, and location in rural or remote areas where the project

   is supporting value chains. It will be a cloud-based application that has the capacity to take full advantage

   of the latest technology developments, including (a) the use of tablets for agents for regular clients’

   operations (onboarding, cash in, and cash out) and (b) the use of mobile phones for clients (transfers, bill

   payments, and so on). The adoption of a modern DCBS will allow eligible MFIs to fully benefit from the

   regulatory and policy changes under preparation at the regional level (that is, issuance of an instruction

   on branchless banking for MFIs, operationalization of a fully interoperable regional payment system, and

   further liberalization of the access to Unstructured Supplementary Service Data codes.



   71.      This subcomponent will finance the following activities: (a) a feasibility study to assess DCBS

   needs; (b) the preparation of the terms of reference for the procurement of a provider of modern DCBS

   solutions (mutualized if possible); and (c) partial funding for the acquisition of the system by the MFIs

   (including the training of their staff and the cost of data transfer). The preparation of the terms of

   reference will notably build on recent World Bank initiatives that identify MFIs ‘ideal’ digital core banking,

   including ability to support customer status (pending, active, and blacklisted), to onboard customers

   (including through biometric means), to assign customer representatives, to support Know Your

   Customer, to use different accounts (current, saving, and technical), to use SMS to notify clients, and so

   on.32 The project will also finance a share of the cost incurred by the implementation of the upgraded

   DCBS (while the beneficiary MFIs will fully pay for the use of the MIS). Implementation costs will involve

   license acquisition, hardware, and technical assistance to use the new system. Such an approach has been

   recently (or is currently being) implemented, among other countries, in Madagascar (P161491), Senegal

   (P174757), Burkina Faso (P174315), and Mali (P168812).

title: Setting up a Long-Term Investment Facility (LTIF) (US$70 million equivalent)
text:
72.     Through this subcomponent, the LTIF will provide equity and quasi-equity financing to viable

   seed and early stage early-stage start-ups and young SMEs (US$15 million) and large firms engaged in

   green investments (notably those in supported value chains [US$55 million]). Investments will be based

   on a broad investment strategy and will be made alongside private investors (as co-investors) who will

   have the majority shares. Investments can be made directly into start-ups and young SMEs or indirectly

   through investments in funds and investment companies who will subsequently invest in the project

   target companies (start-ups and young SMEs).



   73.     The LTIF will be located at the Deposits and Consignment Fund of Côte d’Ivoire (Caisse des

   Dépôts et Consignation de la Côte d’Ivoire, CDC-CI) and managed by a Technical Secretariat (TS)

   reporting to the CDC-CI General Manager (GM). The CDC-CI is an independent public investment entity

   established by the Government in January 2018 with the main objective to ensure the safe custody and

   secure management of public and private funds and to contribute to the financing of the economy

   through the mobilization of long-term resources. The CDC-CI leverages state funds to support economic

   development (and job creation), by providing support to SMEs and investments in lagging and/or

   structure are detailed in Annex 8.



   74.      An independent Investment Committee (IC) will take all investment decisions on the basis of a

   broad investment strategy endorsed by an Advisory Committee (AC) and approved by the World Bank.

   The CDC-CI GM will report to and be part of the AC which will have an arm’s-length monitoring role of the

   The AC will put in place a five-person IC composed of one independent Board member of CDC-CI and four

title: Reforms to improve the business environment (US$12 million equivalent)
text:
79.     The objective of this subcomponent is to support important business environment reforms

   selected from the Reform Agenda (2020–2022). The 2020–2022 Reform Agenda, led by the Investment

   Promotion Agency (Centre de Promotion des Investissements en Côte d’Ivoire, CEPICI) and validated by the

   Council of Ministers, builds on six years of lessons learned and includes 14 priority projects (see Table 4.1

   in Annex 3). These reforms are crosscutting and will benefit all private firms in Côte d’Ivoire, including in

   the value chains supported by the project (Component 1). The project will initially support four reforms

   highlighted in the table 4.1.



   80.     The project will benefit from the experience and institutionalized coordination role of CEPICI,

   which already has committees set up for each of these reform areas as well as developed and budgeted

   action plans. Each reform area involves a plethora of institutions and actors who will be coordinated by

   CEPICI and who may also be beneficiaries of technical assistance as needed to achieve results.



   81.     The project will initially support the following four business environment improvement areas

   (see table in Annex 3):

      (a)   Generalization of the unique identifier of companies in the interior of the country (US$4

            million). The unique identifier will improve the interface between firms and the Government—

            for example, registration, licensing, and taxes. The project will finance the digitization of the

            CEPICI One-stop Shop in Abidjan and support the creation of a second one in Bouaké. Technical

            assistance will be extended to the administrative courts in various localities. Other technical

            assistance will be provided to CEPICI for the management and digitization of archives.

      (b)   Rationalization and digitization of business permits and licenses (US$1 million). To streamline

            the process of obtaining business licenses, the Government is setting up a single portal for issuing





                                                                                                        Page 38 of 141


The World Bank

Competitive Value Chains for Jobs and Economic Transformation Project (P172425)







            licenses, certificates, and business permits, including support to the administrative courts. The

            project will finance an exhaustive inventory of all business licenses (currently 308) in Côte d’Ivoire,

            including (i) identifying and screening of licenses according to criteria (for example, legal basis,

            procedures, revenues, taxes and fees for each individual license); (ii) identifying of high-priority

            licenses and quick-win opportunities; and (iii) evaluation of options for simplification,

            consolidation, and rationalization of licenses and the creation and operationalization of the digital

            platform which will consolidate the information concerning the business licenses including the

            portal to obtain these licenses online.

      (c)   Implementation of the collaborative digital platform for building control and removal of the

            requirement for proof of ownership, topographic extract visa, and urban planning certificate

            (US$4 million). To improve the obtaining of building permits, the Government is operationalizing

            the integrated management platform of the Building Permit Window, which includes the

            implementation of the Single Window for Construction Permits (Guichet Unique du permis de

            Construire, GUPC) software. The project will finance a collaborative digital platform which will

            greatly facilitate cooperation between the different agencies involved. It will also finance satellite-

            based monitoring and the digitalization of the land archives (‘archives domaniales’). This reform

            will contribute to the ‘Dealing with construction permits’ indicator of Doing Business, specifically,

            reducing the time (days) to receive a construction permit from 163 days to 100 days.

      (d)   Operationalization of the unique plot identifier and implementation of a unified geographic

            information system (US$3 million). Eighty percent of the disputes at the court level are related

            to land issues. The average time to obtain a Definite Concession Order (Arrêté de Concession

            Définitive, ACD) is 160 days. To facilitate and secure access to land in Côte d’Ivoire, the

            Government is putting in place a unique land tenure identifier. The project will finance the digital

            platform which will generate this unique land tenure identifier as well as the creation of a unified

            geographic information system. This reform would help reduce the time needed to obtain an ACD,

            which is the definitive order given by the Ministry of Construction, Housing, Sanitation and Urban

            Planning (Ministère de la Construction, du Logement, de l’Assainissement et de l’Urbanisme,

            MCLAU) to obtain land title in urban areas in Côte d'Ivoire. This reduction of days to obtain the

            ACD will have a positive impact on the Doing Business ‘Registering Property’ indicator.

title: Reforms to facilitate trade (US$5 million equivalent)
text:
82.     This subcomponent will support trade facilitation reforms, in particular the improvement of the

   Risk Management System and a Regulatory Compliance Plan at Customs and the digitalization and

   implementation of the Sanitary and Phytosanitary (SPS) certification process by the Ministry of Agriculture

   and Rural Development (Ministère de l’Agriculture et du Développement Rural, MINADER). This

   component will complement the IFC Trade Facilitation West Africa program for Côte d’Ivoire. IFC and

   World Bank teams will work jointly together to support the institutions to carry out reforms. Ultimately

   the reforms supported by this sub-component will contribute to reducing the cost and time associated

   with trade.

   (a)      Technical assistance for the revitalization and implementation of the Authorized Economic

            Operators (AEO) program. The AEO program aims to offer simplified customs procedures to

            reliable, socially responsible companies that offer undeniable guarantees in terms of solvency,

            compliance with regulations, file management, and supply chain security, thus enabling the





                                                                                                           Page 39 of 141


The World Bank

Competitive Value Chains for Jobs and Economic Transformation Project (P172425)







            Customs Administration to focus its a priori control efforts on companies with higher risks. The

            target is to increase the number of AEOs from 2 to 10.

   (b)      Support to the Department of Risk, Information, and Value Analysis (DARRV) at Customs to

            develop a more performant determination of customs value. More specifically, the project will

            finance technical assistance and equipment that would support the DARRV to reduce the

            processing time for an economic operator to receive a certificate of value (attestation de valeur).

    (c)     A framework for voluntary compliance to reduce customs controls through the development and

            operationalization of a client database. The objective is to reduce the volume of declarations in

            the red channel from 34 percent to 20 percent.

   (d)      Support the digitalization of the SPS certification process (e-phytosanitary). The delivery of the

            SPS certificate has already been digitalized and is delivered electronically through the Single

            Window for Trade for Côte d’Ivoire (Guichet Unique du Commerce Exterieur, GUCE-CI). However,

            the rest of the process is not yet digitized. The GUCE-CI and MINADER are already preparing for

            the digitization of the rest of the SPS certification process. However, MINADER requires further

            support to strengthen its inspection capacity, which cannot be digitized and can be the weak link

            in the certification process. The strengthening of inspection capacity near the value chain actors

            to be supported by this project will also help improve and expedite the export of products from

            rural areas.

   83.      The subcomponent may support some Customs IT modernization, subject to IT audits and clear

   link to improved risk-based inspection.

title: Reforms to improve access to industrial land (US$10 million equivalent)
text:
84.      This subcomponent will support reforms to provide clearer and more flexible access to

   industrial land as well as technical assistance to the Agency Responsible for the Management and

   Development of Industrial Infrastructure (Agence de Gestion et de Développement des Infrastructures

   Industrielles, AGEDI) and the Industrial Infrastructure Development Fund (Fonds de Développement des

   Infrastructures Industrielles, FODI), the institutions looking after industrial zones. Access to industrial land

   is an essential part of attracting private investment. New industrial zones are not sufficiently developed,

   while existing industrial zones suffer from congestion and/or offer limited/inadequate services. The

   project will finance technical assistance (equipment, training, and communications) to reinforce the

   capacity of AGEDI and FODI. The project will finance the following:

      (a)   The implementation of an Integrated Industrial Land Management System based on a common

            and unique database to better manage the industrial parks and areas under their responsibility.

            This database will include a geographic information system and will be fed with data by AGEDI

            and FODI as well as the various partners.

      (b)   Support for AGEDI and FODI’s economic and financial models. The project will support AGEDI to

            develop a viable economic and financial model for the management of industrial zones. This study

            will also look at how to integrate SMEs into this model. A similar study will be undertaken for

            FODI.

      (c)   Technical studies to upgrade or improve connectivity to existing zones (for example, waste

            management facilities) and develop new ones, whenever possible in partnership with the private





                                                                                                           Page 40 of 141


The World Bank

Competitive Value Chains for Jobs and Economic Transformation Project (P172425)







            sector. The studies may include financing to support the connection of the Akoupé-Zeudji

            Kilometer Marker 24 (Point Kilomètrique 24 [PK24]) Industrial Zone with the new Y4 highway

            which would improve accessibility of the zone.

      (d)   The development and implementation of initiatives to provide investors clear pathways

            (including the obligation to respect environmental and social standards) to regularize and/or

            develop their industrial land in the cases where they are located outside AGEDI’s industrial zones.

      (e)   Support for the institutional capacity of AGEDI, including (i) reinforcing of the human resources

            of AGEDI and (ii) study tours.

title: Sector-specific reforms (US$3 million equivalent)

text:
55.       In the context of a rapidly developing COVID-19 emergency, a Contingent Emergency Response

   Component (CERC) is added to the project structure to allow for quick disbursement of uncommitted

   balances as a crisis response measure for this COVID-19 situation or any future ones. This will have an

   initial zero value but may be financed during the implementation of the project to allow for an agile and

   rapid reallocation of project funds in the event of a natural or man-made crisis or emergency during

   project implementation to address EEs under conditions established in the PIM.



     C.      Project Beneficiaries



   56.     The project will benefit a wide range of beneficiaries, including end users in rural areas, public-

   sector entities and civil servants, the private sector, and the general population:

      (a)   End users of digital services in target areas. The proposed project targets areas where access to

            digital services and the adoption of broadband are lagging. Rural dwellers—including the youth,

            women, and people with disabilities—will benefit from access to affordable broadband internet

            and will be able to procure mobile handsets through subsidies and/or payment facilities. In

            addition, they will benefit from digital literacy training programs and will be able to access public

            services more efficiently through online platforms, as well as to consume online content and

            services tailored to rural communities. The project will also ensure equitable participation of

            marginalized or vulnerable groups in entrepreneurial activities and digital skills training programs

            by alleviating constraints such as financing, care, access, and transportation. Gender- and

            location-disaggregated data on connectivity will also be recorded to monitor and track progress

            on key parameters of digital inclusion.

      (b)   Public-sector entities in target areas. Public hospitals, health care centers, schools, universities,

            CTD, and agricultural centers will benefit from affordable broadband connectivity and quality

            internet access. In addition, entities that promote digital skills and entrepreneurship (for example,

            incubators, accelerators, coworking spaces, and technology parks) will benefit from improved

            connectivity and access, the acquisition of digital equipment, and capacity-building for their staff.

      (c)   Farmers. Selected smallholder farmers will receive input subsidies through E-vouchers. The target

            smallholder farmers include crop and non-crop farmers and pastoralists in the following strategic

            value chains for MINADER and MINEPIA: cassava, rice, coffee, cashew, fish, bovine milk, pork, and





                                                                                                          Page 38 of 92


The World Bank

Acceleration of the Digital Transformation of Cameroon Project (P173240)







            chicken. The targeted number of direct beneficiaries is approximately 35,125 smallholder farmers,

            livestock-rearing farmers, and pastoralists, out of which 20,099 are agricultural smallholder

            farmers and 15,026 are smallholder livestock-rearing farmers and pastoralists. A matching grant

            will also be provided to producer organizations, associations, cooperatives, and farmers to

            promote adoption of digital innovations developed by agritech startups.

      (d)   Startups and entrepreneurs. The most prominent agritech startups and entrepreneurs will be

            selected through an innovation challenge event and will be offered contracts that will enable

            them to expand their services.

      (e)   Governmental agencies and civil servants. MINPOSTEL, MINADER, MINEPIA, ART, and ANTIC will

            be able to procure critical equipment, and they will benefit from capacity building and digital skills

            training. The data-driven agriculture and information systems will strengthen the public policy-

            making tools at the national and regional levels. The enrolled officers in rural agricultural training

            and animation centers will also benefit from digitalization, training, and capacity building.

      (f)   Private market players in the digital and agritech sectors. Private businesses in the target areas

            will get access to broadband and a digitally savvy workforce, and digital market players will benefit

            from an improved business environment. The private agritech sector will also benefit from the

            organization of innovation challenges focused on agriculture, acceleration activities, contracts,

            and matching grants. The e-voucher for agricultural inputs will also support the development of

            digital finance in the country.

      (g)   General population. Nearly every current or future user of telecom and digital services will benefit

            from the legal and regulatory reforms aimed at reducing costs, improving service quality, and

            stimulating investment and innovation. At the macro level, the project will support increased

            economic growth, productivity, and job creation, both within the digital and agricultural sectors

            and through spillover effects on other productive sectors.



     D.      Results Chain



   57.     The table below presents the project’s results chain/theory of change and includes the

   following assumptions:

           (a) The GoC supports the reform of the telecom/broadband sector.

           (b) The Government’s investment in the sector encourages private-sector entry into the market.

           (c) The regulator can fulfill its duties independently, impartially, and effectively.

           (d) Broadband connectivity and cost are the main drivers of user demand.

           (e) Beneficiary farmers who are granted input subsidies through e-vouchers build stronger

                confidence in the use of digital tools for other agricultural activities.

           (f) Agritech entrepreneurs are sufficiently motivated to expand their services to rural farmers

                in remote regions.

     E.       Rationale for World Bank Involvement and Role of Partners



   58.      The World Bank brings long expertise in supporting similar digital projects globally, as well as

   local knowledge. The World Bank’s added value includes (a) technical expertise in enabling policy and

   regulatory frameworks in the telecom/broadband sector, including earlier work in Cameroon telecom and

   a digital economy country diagnostic under the DE4A initiative; (b) technical expertise around the design

   of the e-voucher scheme and the approaches used to scale up DATs and the digital innovation ecosystem

   for agricultural development; (c) the ability to use a range of products and services in support of public-

   and private-sector actors; and (d) the ability to generate more equitable and beneficial development

   outcomes. For example, the e-voucher mechanism has been proposed based on operational experiences

   in Nigeria and Uganda and the analysis of pilot experiences in Mali, Chad, Niger, and Guinea. 82 The

   proposed project will also emulate the proven approaches adopted by the World Bank’s Digital Agriculture

   Africa team (DAT-Africa team) in successfully scaling up digital innovation in agricultural programs through

   World Bank-financed investment projects.83 The World Bank has been supporting digital transformation





   82 AFCW3 Economic Update, Evidence from E-voucher programs in Mali, Niger, Chad and Guinea, Digitizing Agriculture, Spring

   2019, https://openknowledge.worldbank.org/bitstream/handle/10986/31576/Digitizing-Agriculture-Evidence-from-E-Voucher-

   programs-in-Mali-Chad-Niger-and-Guinea.pdf?sequence=1&isAllowed=y.

   83 The DAT-Africa team organized innovation challenges in Kenya and Uganda to select agritech enterprises with demonstrably



   scalable models to address sector challenges of agricultural productivity, market links, financial inclusion, energy, and data

   analytics and agricultural intelligence. In both countries, the team is now working with ecosystem partners to deploy the

   selected enterprises through three ongoing World Bank-supported projects with aggregate investments of US$600 million that









                                                                                                                          Page 40 of 92


The World Bank

Acceleration of the Digital Transformation of Cameroon Project (P173240)







   across six global regions for several decades and has been involved for a long time in Cameroon in both

   the telecom and agricultural sectors.



   59.     There is a strong rationale for the public financing of this project, given the public good nature

   of the benefits derived from the project across social and economic sectors and the potential to increase

   overall inclusion. The project will enable investments in digital connectivity in vital sectors such as

   agriculture, health, and education. In addition, the project will address inclusion concerns in terms of

   gender, disability, geography, and income levels to compensate for market failures and ensure that the

   most vulnerable are not excluded from the social and economic benefits of Cameroon’s digital

   transformation. Moreover, the improved internet connectivity and digital services that are made possible

   through public interventions can dramatically improve Cameroon’s resilience to shocks (for example,

   emergency calls, monitoring and tracking in dangerous areas, enabling digital communication, health

   diagnosis, and distance learning during health crises such as COVID-19).



   60.      Component 1 will seek to establish the conditions to incentivize private sector investment in

   digital services in line with the MFD approach, while Component 2 will finance infrastructure in areas

   where market failures prevent private-sector interventions in the absence of public-sector funding or

   de-risking. A significant improvement of the policy and regulatory environment appears necessary to

   unleash more private investment in the digital sector. Component 1 will aim to establish and perpetuate

   such an environment. In addition, given the lack of incentives for private telecom operators to extend

   digital services to areas and populations for which the financial return prospects are limited or negative,

   public sector co-funding is primordial. Digital services have increasingly become a necessity for

   households and yet remain out of reach for many segments of the population due to accessibility or

   affordability. Reducing this digital divide by increasing coverage, lowering prices, improving service

   quality, and providing mobile devices to the population—especially in underserved regions—can

   significantly close the opportunities gap between population segments.



   61.      Public funding of Component 3 is required given the challenges to scale up DATs in terms of

   capital needs, coordination among stakeholders, and access to data. The development of foundational

   data infrastructures and acceleration of digital agricultural technologies can enable the delivery of farm-

   level, geospatial, and real-time analytics to inform policies and targeted investments by governments,

   agribusinesses, and intermediary service providers. However, scaling up digital agricultural technologies

   involves generating and accessing large-scale national data sets, a costly challenge for any individual

   market player. Even when data sets are affordable, they are not accessible or shareable across silos, and

   private-sector players lack incentives to share private data sets with the broader ecosystem. Public

   interventions are thus needed, especially given that certain types of data have strong public goods

   components and rely on substantial up-front investments in data capture and analytics infrastructures

   that the private sector may be unwilling to subsidize. Public financing to support, enable, and develop the

   innovation ecosystem for digital agriculture also addresses classic coordination failures and offers longer-

   term sustainability returns for both the private sector as well as farmers.

   Inclusive Growth Project (NARIG, P153349) - US$200 million; Kenya Climate-Smart Agriculture Project (KCSAP, P154784) -

   US$250 million; and Uganda Agriculture Cluster Development Project (ACDP) - US$150 million.

The World Bank

Acceleration of the Digital Transformation of Cameroon Project (P173240)







   62.     Component 3 has potential synergies with the work and investments of the International

   Finance Corporation (IFC) in Cameroon. In line with this project and building on its current portfolio, IFC

   plans to step up support to the private agriculture sector, including tools such as rural finance, crop

   insurance, and warehouse receipts. The World Bank will build on this project along with IFC on future

   Advisory Services and Analytics to support private investment in agriculture. IFC will continue supporting

   agriculture finance, in particular through its investments in Banque Internationale du Cameroun pour

   l’Epargne et le Crédit (BICEC) and SFC Agri RSF (Risk Sharing Facility established by BICEC), which have

   been financing credit lines to farmers while strengthening value chains and competitiveness. Under

   Subcomponent 3.3, the World Bank will leverage IFC’s expertise to provide a matchmaking program

   (previously done through TechEmerge) that connects companies worldwide with leading organizations in

   emerging markets.



   63.      The project complements existing programs run by partner organizations that support

   agricultural development in Cameroon. The International Fund for Agricultural Development financed

   several activities with a similar focus on digital innovation and youth, including the Program for the

   Promotion of Agropastoral Youth Entrepreneurship, the Commodity Value Chain Support Project, and the

   Aquaculture Entrepreneurship Promotion Project. The African Development Bank is another potential

   partner for livestock and fish farming value chains (Livestock and Fish Farming Value Chains Development

   Project through the Agricultural Value Chain Development Project. Other partners include the French

   Development Agency (Agence Française de Développement, AFD), the Japan International Cooperation

   Agency (JICA), and the German International Cooperation Agency (Deutsche Gesellschaft für

   Internationale Zusammenarbeit, GIZ). AFD carried out a program for the development of vocational

   training in the agricultural, livestock, and fishing sectors and the Improvement of the Competitiveness of

   Agricultural Family Farming Program. JICA invests heavily in the rice sector through the Project for the

   Development of Irrigated and Rainfed Rice Cultivation, and GIZ operates the green innovation centers for

   the Agriculture and Food Sector project. The project could also collaborate with the ongoing World Bank-

   financed Rural Electricity Access Project for Underserved Regions (P163881) to increase productive uses

   of energy in agriculture.



     F.      Lessons Learned and Reflected in the Project Design



   64.      A focused approach to materialize the transformative impact of digital services in one sector

   only is more efficient than a broad approach across several verticals. A broad approach that would tackle

   the digital transformation of several sectors at once would spread out resources, complicate coordination,

   and likely produce fewer results. Comparable projects, such as the Safe Schooling and Distance Education

   Project (P173997) in Turkey and the Côte d’Ivoire E-Agriculture Project (P160418), have focused their

   efforts on one sector in addition to the foundational digital/ICT sector. Through Component 3, the

   proposed project focuses solely on the digitalization of the agricultural sector and aims to use this vertical

   as a proof of concept to later extend the intervention to other sectors that could benefit from digital

   transformation.



   65.    While focused in terms of socioeconomic sectors addressed, the approach still must be

   comprehensive on both the supply and demand sides. The project draws on the World Bank’s vast

   experience in digital infrastructure investments and telecom market reform, as well as on a growing body
