C. Project Beneficiaries



53. The NYOTA Project is expected to impact 800,000 vulnerable youth aged 18-29 across all 47 counties of Kenya

    including 10,000 refugees and 10,000 vulnerable host community members. The project beneficiaries are targeted

    youth aged 18-29, with little or no education,68 who are unemployed, underemployed, or in low-tier employment

    with very low earnings. There are 2.4 million youth aged 18-29 among the poorest 40 percent of Kenyans who fulfil

     one or more of these criteria. As such, the project will cover 35 percent of this pool of potentially eligible youth. Such

     youth face exclusions and are often unable to access government sponsored jobs programs. The project will reserve

     50 percent of slots for female beneficiaries and 5 percent for people with disabilities. Women face additional barriers

     to participate in the labor force, to access better quality employment, to earn what a man would earn in an identical

     job, and when they start up and run their own businesses. People with disabilities also have additional barriers across

     the life cycle, in education, in employment, and face negative attitudes and strong stigma. Given delays with acquiring

     education, the target age group for persons with disabilities is expanded to 18-35. Officials from participating

     government implementing institutions will directly benefit from professional capacity building, technology upgrade,

     systems enhancement, and monitoring and evaluation support.



D. Results Chain



54. The project aims to address barriers that vulnerable youth face in accessing better employment and earnings. The

    project’s theory of change is illustrated in Figure 2. Youth with lower levels of educational attainment lack the soft

    skills, basic skills such as reading, writing, digital skills, as well as more advanced technical skills needed to get good

    jobs or to set up thriving micro-enterprises. Women face further time-use barriers given care responsibilities and

    gender norms. People with disabilities and refugees face even greater barriers as outlined previously. The NYOTA

    project provides integrated interventions that address these constraints. Interventions that tackle both the lack of

    skills along various dimensions (socio-emotional, cognitive, technical, digital), on-the-job training, and job search

    support helps increase beneficiaries’ productivity and helps them find good jobs. Well-designed apprenticeship

    programs designed closely with private sector employers can help ease the transition from school to work.69 Similarly

    NYOTA offers multi-faceted support to starting businesses – including providing financing, business training,

    addressing behavioral facets, and connecting to networks. An ongoing impact evaluation of this intervention in the

    KYEOP project shows its effectiveness in leading to successful self-employment.70 For youth who are particularly

    hard-to-reach, the thriving social enterprise sector in Kenya offers solutions. Some examples include Kidogo, which

    trains women in quality childcare provision and helps them become "mamapreneurs”; and Solar Sister, working with

    women in rural areas helping these ‘solar entrepreneurs’ with providing last mile access/service to quality solar

    products. These interventions are expected to move beneficiaries from inactivity/unemployment/underemployment

    into better quality jobs/more productive enterprises in the short term.



55. The project further aims to facilitate youth savings. Vulnerable youth lack good schemes in which to save when they

    are able to and build a cushion which can be used to start a business or when facing adversities. They also often lack

    financial awareness to understand the importance of savings. The NYOTA project will address the key design,

    behavioral, and operational constraints that limit the participation of vulnerable youth in savings schemes.

    International experience suggests that the poor save, even in long-term schemes, if these schemes are easy,

    convenient, flexible, trusted, incentivized, and provide tangible short-term benefits.71 In the short term, this will lead

    to improved savings habits among youth and greater financial awareness.

title: Development of Advanced and Intermediate Digital Skills (US$45 million)
text:
27.      This subcomponent aims to enhance intermediate and advanced digital skills in close collaboration with the

private sector and with the support of the World Bank Education team and IFC. Phase 1 will support the development of

digital competencies required in both the public and private sectors, with a particular focus on empowering youth and

boosting women’s enrollment in beneficiary programs. Subcomponent 1.2 will also support the existing digital skills

training academies for public servants, especially those involved in the digitalization initiatives supported by Phase 1, and

will draw lessons from other countries, such as Ghana and Madagascar, to support the digital skills curriculum

development and foster investments in education, while also assuring the application of all applicable and appropriate

data protection, privacy, and user-consent policies.

28.       A significant portion of the investments under this subcomponent will be allocated to ESATIC, supervised by

the MTND34. Over the last 10 years, ESATIC has trained over 1,700 graduates with a 90 percent employability rate and

3,000 private sector executives. However, ESATIC overall capacity needs to be expanded to meet industry and public

administration demands. Approximately US$30 million will be dedicated to works and renovation costs to support

ESATIC’s extension to double its graduate capacity from 250 to 500 graduates annually and respond to the needs of the

digital labor market. This includes refurbishing student housing; upgrading laboratories with advanced AI, Big Data, and



29

    In the medium term, the Government contemplates the establishment of a structure (agency, office, and so on) with a unique and independent mandate and

capabilities. Such a structure would monitor, supervise, coordinate, and enforce AI legislation, standards, model evaluations, and so on.

30 An AI governance framework includes policies, processes, and structures for AI system development and monitoring, addressing accountability, regulation



compliance, ethics, risk management, stakeholder roles, and decision-making. An AI Model Evaluation supports the AI governance framework by ensuring models meet

quality standards (accuracy, reliability, fairness). It assesses resource requirements, data management, security protocols, and cost implications.

31

   AfDB supports resource mutualization and interministerial coordination and Phase 1 can further assist in shaping a cohesive strategy that leverages all data center

infrastructure for secure government hosting with recognized standards (for example, ISO 27001 or Tier III) and flexible data localization guidelines.

32 This includes diagnostic studies, standards to reduce GHG emissions, climate resilience, network redundancies, and disaster recovery.

33 In 2015, Côte d’Ivoire became a member of the Open Government Partnership (OGP), a multilateral initiative to promote open government and improve governance.

34

    Two other schools under the MTND also provide some advanced trainings in ICT: EMSP and the Institute of Communication Sciences and Techniques (Institut des

Sciences et Techniques de la Communication Polytechnique, ISTC).

AR/VR equipment; and constructing two new buildings: one for additional classrooms and a library and another as a

women-only dormitory to boost female enrollment. A partnership with IFC for a pilot D4TEP, an acceleration program to

support digital transformation of organizations, will be explored to support ESATIC. The High Multinational School of Posts

(Ecole Multinationale Supérieure des Postes, EMSP) will also benefit from minor rehabilitation of classrooms. Finally,

technical studies will examine different options for size, viability, and opportunities to define and implement PPPs to

involve the private sector in covering the school's operational costs. Phase 1 will also fund merit scholarships and

specialized training for professors, young women, and people with disabilities from rural areas to enroll in intermediate

and advanced digital programs.

29.        Other key activities to be financed under this subcomponent include TA, non-consulting services, and goods:

     (a)   Enhancing the supply of advanced digital skills training by building partnerships with the private sector. (i) TA

           for the MTND to conduct studies35 to gather statistics on digital skills in Côte d'Ivoire and develop strong

           partnerships between the MTND, innovation hubs, the technology industry (both local and international), and

           tertiary education institutions. By establishing these partnerships, this activity will aim to build a collaborative

           framework for digital skills development, thus enhancing youth employability and mobilizing PCE/PCM.36 IFC and

           the World Bank will conduct a digital skills mapping exercise in collaboration with the Government and the private

           sector during implementation. (ii) TA activities and equipment provision to ESATIC, EMSP, the Félix Houphouët-

           Boigny National Polytechnic Institute (Institut National Polytechnique Félix Houphouët-Boigny, INP-HB),37 the

           Virtual University, and other selected institutions, in collaboration with the private sector and international higher

           education providers. The goal is to increase their program offerings (quantity and quality) and capacity to deliver

           specialized and advanced programs in areas, such as cybersecurity, data science (AI and machine learning [ML]),

           augmented/virtual reality, fiber-optic, programming, and information systems.

     (b)   Training civil servants to support behavioral change. TA for development and support (operational costs and

           equipment) and for the implementation and expansion of government-wide digital upskilling and reskilling

           programs to cover 35,000 civil servants over five years.38 This would help ensure the success of the Government’s

           digital transformation and change management in priority sectors (for example, justice, health, social protection,

           civil registration, and education). To support behavioral change, Phase 1 will follow a comprehensive approach

           that combines targeted training with strategic interventions to support change management such as coaching,

           peer networks, and mentoring.

     (c)   Training and upskilling the work force to meet the needs of the digital jobs market. TA and extensive

           intermediate and advanced learning programs to train over 35,000 certified individuals in close collaboration with

           the private sector, major technology companies, and various local education institutions (including ESATIC, the

           International Telecommunication Union [ITU] Digital Transformation Center hosted by EMSP, and the National

           Virtual University). The TA will define a sustainable framework for the delivery of these certifications, based on a

           hybrid approach (virtual and physical training depending on specialization) and by leveraging the abovementioned

           institutions’ facilities and equipment. This activity will be complemented by PPP-based models, such as edtech

           bootcamps and industry partnerships, for shorter, job-oriented certifications.

text:

30.      This subcomponent will provide broadband internet access to priority public facilities already connected to

electricity. The Program will connect 1,400 education institutions (600 under Phase 1 and 800 under Phase 2); 1,000 health

establishments (400 under Phase 1 and 600 under Phase 2); 39 courthouses under Phase 1; 121 social centers (59 social

centers under Phase 1 and 62 under Phase 2); and 400 city halls/sub-prefectures (250 under Phase 1 and 150 under Phase

2). This activity will also cover the regional directorates of the Ministries of Education, Ministry of Health and the MPSAM.

The last-mile connectivity provided under this subcomponent will benefit from the capacity-building program for civil

servants planned under Component 1, thereby ensuring the effective uptake of broadband use. The Program will work in

close collaboration with the National Electricity Digitalization and Access (NEDA P176776) Project and complementary

initiatives under the M300 Energy Compact to identify newly electrified facilities for broadband connectivity.

31.      Phase 1 aims to generate an additional US$10 million in PCM through the deployment of fiber, mobile, and

satellite connectivity solutions. Phase 1 will promote PCM through designing interventions that crowd-in private sector

funding and stimulate private sector development. It will use a mix of fiber-optic cables, mobile, and satellite broadband

to ensure comprehensive coverage. Fiber-optic cables with climate-proofing features will connect institutions near fiber

backbones, whereas mobile and satellite broadband will reach remote areas. It is estimated that Phase 1 will mobilize

US$10 million in additional investment, with an average ratio of 1:3 for public and private sector financing. It will unlock

private investment through procurement of connectivity services where private operators will complement the required

capital expenditure (CAPEX) to extend networks with fiber backbones, mobile towers, and ground stations for satellites.

32.     Key activities to be financed under this subcomponent include the following:

  (a)   The TA will prepare the technical grounds through (i) mapping and geospatial analysis of public facilities, including

        health centers and education institutions, with their electrification status and associated climate risks; (ii)

        recommendations on open access policies and sharing of passive infrastructure to facilitate last mile network

        rollout and incentivize private sector operators to invest in last-mile connectivity to households; (iii) identification

        of the priority public institutions (within the education, health, and civil registry sectors) that will benefit from a

        new/upgraded digital connectivity, in synergies with other World Bank-financed projects; (iv) a feasibility study to

        define user requirements for internet bandwidth and indoor connectivity solutions (incorporating specific needs

        to ensure business continuity for key government functions during crises such as the COVID-19 pandemic or

        natural/climate disasters) to be provided by the private sector, in consultation with relevant line ministries; and

        (v) preparation of the bidding documents for digital connectivity to be provided by the private sector (connectivity

        will be procured as much as possible through the ‘reverse auctions’ mechanisms implemented by the closed e-

        Agriculture Project [P160418] to generate PCM).

  (b)   Acquisition and financing of connectivity services and equipment, including end-user devices, in identified

        locations. Connectivity will be purchased for public facilities, along with a comprehensive outdoor and indoor

        broadband solution package including IT equipment, as well as installation and maintenance to the selected

        beneficiaries. Basic maintenance and troubleshooting training will be delivered to local IT technicians and end-

        users to ensure the sustainability of this activity. Phase 1 will also explore affordable pricing models for devices

        (through a combination of market and policy reforms to achieve lower retail data and device prices).

title: Protection and Resilience of Critical Infrastructure (US$15 million)
text:
33.    This subcomponent will aim to update and operationalize the Critical Infrastructure Protection Plan (CIPP) and

support the decommissioning of abandoned and vulnerable radioelectric sites. Phase 1 will support the updating and

implementation of the CIPP,39 adopted by Decree No. 2021–916. The implementation will aim to enhance the resilience

and security of critical infrastructure, addressing both current and emerging threats, as well as ensuring a secure and

reliable infrastructure network across critical sectors. Furthermore, Phase 1 will strengthen the capacity of the National

Emergency Telecommunications Plan (NETP), developed in 2018, by leveraging existing public and private networks. This

subcomponent will support the decommissioning of 552 abandoned telecommunications towers that pose significant

threats to local populations.40 This activity has been identified as a priority by the GoCI following the recent deadly incident

in Korhogo, where severe weather conditions caused the collapse of mobile phone towers. Many of these sites were

previously owned by now-bankrupt mobile operators and have been abandoned since their licenses were revoked 10

years ago due to noncompliance with regulatory requirements. IFC will contribute to identifying private sector solutions

to address this issue.

 34.       Key activities to be financed under this subcomponent include the following:

     (a)   TA to increase digital resilience with (i) a comprehensive mapping of critical infrastructure and the development

           of an implementation road map of the CIPP, as well as business continuity plans and capacity-building activities

           and (ii) supporting the NETP, which will include an assessment of the state of the organizational structure and the

           definition of policies and regulations for emergency telecommunications in the country in case of disaster.

     (b)   Cybersecurity audits and investments (mainly software and some hardware) for selected Security Operations

           Centers (SOCs) for critical infrastructures.

     (c)   The decommissioning and dismantling of 552 abandoned telecommunications sites to mitigate any danger they

           may present, as they pose significant risks to public safety.

     (d)   TA to review the regulatory framework and take necessary actions to reduce the risks of further incidents related

           to abandoned telecommunication sites and create a safer environment for populations by (i) updating existing

           regulations and strengthening construction standards to ensure the stability of telecommunications towers under

           extreme conditions; (ii) strengthening monitoring and enforcement mechanisms with the involvement of local

           communities; and (iii) promoting sustainable management of radioelectric infrastructure and e-waste.

text:

title: Access to and Inclusion in Digital Public Services (US$25 million)
text:
37.      This subcomponent aims to deploy new access channels for remote and vulnerable populations so that they

will benefit from the availability of digitally enabled public services. This subcomponent will fund the pilot phase for

deploying both physical and mobile digital user centers (MSP) to evaluate various service delivery models and support the

goal of deploying 509 MSPs in every sub-prefecture. The deployment of MSPs will be sequenced based on demographics,

coverage, readiness, and other key criteria, starting with the capital Abidjan, and then moving on to urban areas, large

infrastructural hubs, and so on. MPSs will be coupled with mobile caravans that will serve as dynamic hubs for learning,

engagement, and community development. Phase 1 also includes targeted interventions to address the needs of women,

vulnerable communities, and persons with disabilities (PwDs) by providing information and services are provided in a

nondiscriminatory and accessible manner, while ensuring application of appropriate data protection, privacy, and user-

consent policies.

38.        Key activities to be financed under this subcomponent include the following:

     (a)   Support to delivery channels of public services: (i) TA and capacity building for enhancing government service

           delivery channels, both in-person and virtual (website), to enhance inclusive access, including features for PwDs;44

           (ii) deployment of 15 MSPs in the select regions through renovation costs,45 hardware and IT equipment,46 TA,

           capacity building, and impact evaluation for the pilot phase;47 (iii) support for renovation costs, hardware and IT

           equipment, TA, and capacity-building for digitizing and archiving civil registration data for the effective

           implementation of the CityWeb software, as well as the deployment of electronic kiosks in 50 municipalities and

           civil registry centers; and (iv) support for the opening of civil registry offices and the deployment of the mobile

           registration application in hospitals in rural areas, which will serve as the first access point for birth registration

           and the issuance of NNIs in close collaboration with the Health MPA (P179550) to identify beneficiaries.

     (b)   Outreach activities: (i) acquisition of IT equipment and delivery of training programs for young people as ‘Digital

           Ambassadors’ to support communities and lead local campaigns in communication efforts to enhance the use of

           digital services, primarily in the MSPs and/or through national training center programs and (ii) deployment of

           mobile caravans in rural areas, in collaboration with the private sector and accredited public institutions,48 to

           provide targeted basic digital skills education for women and underserved populations, including PwDs. The goal

           is to reach 300,000 beneficiaries over five years, thereby empowering them to effectively access and utilize public

           services, while also fostering inclusive digital adoption with the use of AI solutions.

     (c)   Content production to support outreach activities: development of communication content specifically tailored

           to educate and raise awareness about the use of digital public services. This will include a variety of multimedia

           supports (images, comics, local radios) and social media channels/networks. Particular attention will be paid to

           the development of relevant content for illiterates, women, older people, and PwDs.

title: Upgrading Financial Management, Procurement, and Oversight (US$8.40 million IDA
text:
equivalent)

      32.    The objective of this sub-component is to support the modernization and streamlining of fiduciary

      systems, enabling the AUC to benefit from the efficiency and improved productivity of integrated FM systems.

Building Institutions And Systems to Harness And Realize Agenda 2063 Project (P180117)







This will enable the AUC to establish itself as a Center of Excellence in FM and transfer its institutional knowledge

and experience to its regional offices and bodies. The AUC has well-established FM and internal control systems

that are supported by policies, procedures, financial regulations, manuals, and guidelines. However, it has

struggled to meet the required level of efficiency and effectiveness. The first World Bank project supported some

elements of FM systems. However, it did not go deep enough in terms of tackling the foundational problems that

undermine effective and efficient FM. This sub-component will support: (i) investment in modern tools and

policies for the effective planning and financial information consolidation to improve budget preparation, audit,

results monitoring, and grant management; (ii) the implementation of a structured mid-year budget review to

enable course correction in the course of a financial year; (iii) enterprise risk management; (iv) the strengthening

of professional collaborations in regional accounting; (v) the automation of procurement, payment systems,

processes, and accounting, for example through integration with banks by enforcing applicability and updating all

relevant financial regulations, frameworks, systems, and manuals; (vi) the strengthening of internal oversight; (vii)

capacity building of staff in audit, financial management, and procurement; (viii) the upgrading of policies and

tools for warehouse management and asset tracking; (ix) and the development, implementation, and certification

to International Organization for Standardization (ISO) 9001:2015 quality management system (QMS).

33.      This sub-component will also finance improvements in the AUC’s procurement policies, practices, and

systems to improve efficiency and value for money. The AUC aims to evolve its procurement function into a

technically capable and efficient supply chain management system. It would be equipped with skilled technical

experts that can deliver the required best quality service and output within a reasonable time frame. Under this

sub-component, the project will finance the final phase of e-procurement started under the first project. The aim

will be to enhance the organization’s capacity in undertaking procurement processes for goods, works and

services. The project will finance the provision of training; the piloting and roll out of e-procurement at the AUC;

and system integration. The project will also finance staff capacity building and improvements in asset

management. The Operations Support Services Directorate (OSSD) has prepared a new procurement manual,

Strategic Plan, and Service-Level Agreements. The Directorate also plans to train all users across business units, as

well as suppliers. The AUC standard operating procedures and Staff Rules and Regulations (including travel

policies) will change as part of the ongoing reforms. These changes call for continued skill development, system

enhancements, and the updating of operating procedures. These measures will help to fully professionalize the

AUC’s procurement function to match best international practices.

title: Innovations to improve Human Resource Management (US$4.25 million IDA equivalent)
text:
34.        The objective of this sub-component is to improve HRM functionality at the AUC. The sub-component

will: (i) support the Directorate of Human Resource Management to improve its recruitment policies, rules, and

procedures; (ii) improve talent and performance through leadership and capacity building for AU staff; and (iii)

develop a fair and efficient HRM, including a performance appraisal system. This sub-component will finance

innovations in technology and HRM practices to enable the AUC staff and management to change the existing

working culture and establish a high-performing and competent cadre of staff. This is in line with the AUC’s vision

to evolve into a “high-performing efficient and effective organization that is able to deliver on agreed continental

priorities, attract and retain the best quality staff at all levels, while operating within a strong accountability and

performance-based framework”. Activities to be financed include the following: (i) the development and

implementation of a HRMIS; (ii) the deployment of the AUC document management system; (iii) the review and

revision of HR policies, including gender activities to support parity; (iv) the development and implementation of

a 360-degree performance appraisal program; (v) the development and implementation of the AUC Employee

Learning Program; (vi) the revamping of the recruitment function; (vii) project coordination to support the rollout

of the AU transition plan; and (viii) the strengthening of internal communications.

title: Improving functionality and performance of ICT systems (US$6.34 million IDA equivalent)
text:
35.      The objective of this sub-component is to support the modernization of the AUC’s ICT systems by

improving their functionality and performance. Specifically, the AUC intends to: (i) modernize the IT

infrastructure; (ii) improve capacity for application development; (iii) enhance professional development; and (iv)

strengthen IT security. The AUC has established ana NOC with limited capacity to partially monitor, operate, and

maintain some of the services it provides. The NOC requires additional enhancement to attain comprehensive

24/7 proactive monitoring, as well as to maintain the availability of all services. Enhancing the NOC will

significantly improve the business continuity of the organization through proactive management of incidents, as

well as a calculated planning of system capacity and utilization. This would enable the system to maintain: (i)

improved service availability and reduced downtime; (ii) improvements in system performance; (iii) maximization

of return on investment; and (iv) planned timely upgrades.

36.      Considering the vast range of services that the Management Information Service Directorate (MISD)

provides to various AU departments, there is a need for continual IT infrastructure improvement. These

improvements range from optimizing processes, to architecture amendments, to the upgrading of the ICT

infrastructure. The upgrading process will improve the current network performance and security, as well as

eliminate vendor support management issues resulting from the installation of equipment from different vendors.

The AUC intends to replace the outdated network equipment and upgrade the IT Infrastructure at the Regional

Offices, Organs, and Local Offices to enhance communications within and outside of the AU. This infrastructure

enhancement will improve the overall infrastructure and data security of the Union. It will also contribute to the

process of aligning the AUC to international data security standards. The project will also invest in staff skills and

capacity development, as well as develop new tools for management. To this end, the proposed project will

support the following activities: (i) the establishment of a security operations center and enhancement of the

NOC; (ii) the enhancement of IT wired and wireless network infrastructure performance and security; (iii) the

upgrade of network infrastructure; (iv) the replacement of IT equipment and tools; (v) the data warehouse and

business intelligence; (vi) the supply of telephony equipment; and (vii) the revamping of the existing ERP system.

title: Supporting the implementation of the AfCFTA Treaty (US$17.45 million IDA equivalent)
text:
38.      The objective of this sub-component is to support the strengthening of the AfCFTA Secretariat in

facilitating the implementation of the AfCFTA Treaty. With 54 State Parties, the AfCFTA is the regional trade

agreement with the most signatories in the world. Further, the AfCFTA is not only a free trade agreement

regulating trade in goods, but also covers trade in services, investment, competition policy, intellectual property

rights and digital trade. Thus, the AfCFTA goes beyond most existing REC agreements in terms of its thematic

coverage, comprising issues, which for many African countries are going to be subject to new international trade



                                                                                                           Page 18 of 59


The World Bank

Building Institutions And Systems to Harness And Realize Agenda 2063 Project (P180117)







discipline for the first time. This requires significant investment in activating the institutional framework for the

functioning of the Treaty, as well as in supporting Treaty implementation to realize the AfCFTA objectives and

benefits.

39.     Although most of the implementation of the AfCFTA and related reforms need to be undertaken at the

Member State level, the success of the Treaty will depend on the support provided by the AfCFTA Secretariat

to ensure coherence, coordination and effective compliance. Thus, the AfCFTA Secretariat will need to build its

capacity to provide various services to its membership to support the effective implementation of the Treaty on

the ground. The proposed project aims to strengthen the capacity of the AfCFTA Secretariat to ensure that the

commitments made by countries, many of which have limited implementation capacity, are fully implemented

and coupled with a parallel agenda to maximize the potential benefits of the AfCFTA. To do this, the proposed

project will support selected aspects of the following activities: (i) strengthening institutional capacity of the

AfCFTA Secretariat, including finalization of remaining annexes and the built in agendas; (ii) conclusion of the

negotiations for the outstanding protocols; (iii) trade facilitation, customs, and transit aspects; (iv) trade in

services, investment promotion and facilitation, digital trade, and intellectual property rights; (v) the

harmonization of standards, promoting equivalence and mutual recognition, the collection of non-tariff measures

data, addressing non-tariff barriers, and the promotion of competition policy and trade remedies; (vi) the

development and implementation of the DSM, rules of procedure, and related training; (vii) monitoring of

commitments through trade policy reviews, and capacity building of NICs; (viii) capacity building of staff; and (ix)

the purchase of equipment.

title: Supporting the implementation of the SAATM (US$5.50 million IDA equivalent)
text:
40.     The objective of this sub-component is to support the AUC in coordinating the implementation of the

SAATM Treaty. To achieve a truly competitive air transport market in Africa that advances the common interest

of regional integration, the member states’ solemn commitment to the SAATM Treaty set an expectation of

removing limitations on air traffic, easing access rights, and fostering partnerships that can improve connectivity

for travelers and traders. This needs to be complemented with better policy frameworks, both regionally and

domestically, adequate safety and security standards, and enhanced market connectivity to raise productivity and

encourage investment and innovation.

41.      The support under this sub-component will follow a two-pronged approach to ensure that the AUC and

the specialized agencies of the AU can accelerate their efforts to: (i) increase the number of countries that are

signatories of the SAATM by developing and disseminating evidence of the socioeconomic benefits of

liberalization and competition, and (ii) deepen liberalization in member states that are already signatories of the

SAATM, particularly in the 20 member states that have signed the memorandum of implementation. Project

activities will strengthen the AUC, AFCAC, and AfCFTA Secretariat. Specifically, they will strengthen these

organizations’ capacity to facilitate and monitor the implementation of States’ commitments related to the

liberalization of air services, and the broader development of air transport systems, with an expectation of

enhancing regional connectivity and intracontinental trade in Africa. Additionally, activities will also increase

engagement and accountability among States and key stakeholders by improving transparency and openness with

reporting to the monitoring body of the YD, the private sector, development partners, civil society and other

stakeholders. This would be done in collaboration with the RECs.

42.     The proposed project will support the following activities: (i) advocacy for domestication and

harmonization of YD principles in member countries; (ii) operationalizing the SAATM Dispute Settlement

Secretariat and Mechanism; (iii) the development of a continent-wide aviation data and statistics reporting

system, the African Program on Aviation Data; (iv) the completion of a gap analysis of the air navigation services



                                                                                                          Page 19 of 59


The World Bank

Building Institutions And Systems to Harness And Realize Agenda 2063 Project (P180117)







infrastructure, and the development of a comprehensive airspace and air navigation/aviation infrastructure

investment plan; (v) the development of a framework for the reduction of air transport taxes and fees to boost

trade and the movement of people; (vi) the development of the Africa Air Cargo Development Strategy; and (vii)

the preparation of a Multimodal Transport Analysis and Modelling.

title: Supporting the implementation of the FMP (US$2 million IDA equivalent)
text:
43.     The objective of this sub-component is to support the AUC’s effort to accelerate the ratification and

implementation readiness of the Protocol on the FMP. This support builds on recent gains in the advancement

of the FMP agenda, as it contributes to the implementation of measures required to enhance the movement of

African people for education, tourism, and trade. Capacity building will be supported to enable the AUC to better

manage the signature and ratification of the protocol by member states.

44.      To facilitate this process, support will also be needed to raise the member states’ awareness concerning

the benefits of the FMP through advocacy, sensitization and training of national authorities and stakeholders.

In addition, considering that the full implementation of the FMP is dependent upon the operationalization of the

African Passport for a visa-free Africa, capacity support will be provided to the AUC for the promotion of

streamlined identity and civil registration systems in members states, including the modernization of ID

technologies so that the number of persons with government-issued proof of identity can be increased. The

proposed project will support the AUC in better managing the signature and ratification by member states of the

Protocol on the FMP, raising awareness of the benefits of the FMP through advocacy. It would also support

measures to deal with institutional and procedural concerns that inhibit progress on the FMP Protocol. Specific

activities to be supported include: (i) advocacy activities for the accelerated ratification of the FMP Protocol in

pending countries; (ii) the establishment of framework principles and policies to facilitate border management;

(iii) support for the development of shared databases to facilitate border management among member states;

(iv) technical assistance to harmonize policies on free movement between the RECs and state parties (for example,

a one-stop border check); and (v) facilitating the movement of business persons for trade and investment to

support the implementation of the AfCFTA agreement.

title: Sustainable, climate resilient and community-led fisheries management (US$31 million, of which
text:
US$24 million IDA, US$4.5 million equivalent AFD, US$2.5 million PROBLUE) . This component seeks to enhance

community-led management initiatives and provide tools for sustainable and climate-resilient fisheries management in

Guinea.

26.     Sub-component 1.1 Strengthening fisheries governance (US$20 million, of which US$18 million IDA, US$1 million

equivalent AFD, US$1 million PROBLUE). This sub-component aims to strengthen fisheries governance and management.

The interventions will support the development and enforcement of science-based regulations to ensure the sustainable

exploitation of endangered fish stocks, including through community-led fisheries management arrangements between

the government and small-scale fisheries organizations or communities. In addition, the project will develop or strengthen

the legal framework and mechanism to secure sustainable financing to support the government’s fisheries management

services.

27.     Fisheries management plans. The project will support the development and monitoring of fisheries management

plans through support to the CNSHB for provision of scientific advice based on fisheries-dependent data (e.g., geolocated

catch and effort statistics, size distribution of catch of main species) and fisheries-independent data (e.g., stock abundance

indexes through regular scientific campaigns, biological data on main marine and freshwater species). Additionally, the

project will support the MPEM in consulting stakeholders and implementing an ongoing monitoring and evaluation

framework for fisheries management plans. At the local level, the project will expand community-led fisheries

management initiatives piloted under the WARFP (P126773) by providing technical assistance packages to establish

community-led fisheries management associations, and equipment for participatory monitoring of fisheries activities,

including operational resources.28 To address the gender gap in voice and agency, the project will encourage the

establishment of quotas for women’s representation in executive management bodies (as chairperson, treasurer, etc.)

and community-led fisheries management initiatives. This will be achieved by: (i) supporting the preparation of a decree

that promotes the representation of women in community-led fisheries management associations; and (ii) establishing a

28.      Monitoring, control, and surveillance (MCS) and transparency. The project will strengthen the MCS system

implemented by the CNSP through capacity building and management of fishing capacity (including registration of

artisanal vessels, semi-industrial and industrial vessels, verification of their technical characteristics, fishing licenses,

geolocation of artisanal boats, electronic fishing logbook for industrial fishing vessels, renovation and modernization of

CNSP's patrol resources, strengthened legal framework).29 Additionally, the project will support initiatives for improved

transparency related to fisheries governance, including the development of a comprehensive information system on

fisheries and aquaculture (including the adequacy between supply and demand in a context of rapid change due to the

development of Simandou) and technical assistance for Guinea’s compliance with international initiatives, including the

Fisheries Transparency Initiative and the Global Fishing Watch initiative. 30

29.     Institutional capacity building. The project will enhance the operational capacities of the technical directorates

of the MPEM and of its supporting technical agencies (CNSHB, CNSP, ANAG, ONSPA) through staff training, provision of

legal support to strengthen the legal framework in alignment with international standards, and establishment of

cooperation mechanisms between institutions to improve information exchange, including through the development of

information systems. The project will also support strategic studies for the sector, such as assessing the fisheries potential

of inland water bodies, conducting technical studies to support a UN-recognized delineation of the limits of the Exclusive

Economic Zone (EEZ) and developing a sectoral environmental and social impact assessment.

title: Research, innovation and conservation for climate resilient fisheries (US$11 million
text:
equivalent, of which US$6 million IDA, US$3.5 million equivalent AFD, US$1.5 million PROBLUE). This sub-component

aims to improve the integration of climate change considerations into fisheries and aquaculture management to enhance

the climate resilience of these sectors. The sub-component will include the following activities:

31.      Management of Marine and Coastal Protected Areas as a Nature-based Solution (NBS) for coastal resilience and

fish nurseries by strengthening the management framework of Marine Protected Areas. This includes demarcation,

zoning, and stakeholder consultations to strengthen the network of Marine Protected Areas. Additionally, it involves

operational support for OGPNRF eco-guards to conduct patrols that mitigate ecosystem degradation, financing of patrols,

acquisition of technical and camping equipment, acquisition of vehicles, and rehabilitation of base camps. Activities,

conducted in partnership with Non-governmental Organization (NGOs), will support Marine Protected Areas’ governance,

local natural resources management, ecosystem restoration and sustainable income generating activities.

32.      Multiannual scientific research programs on both marine protected areas and freshwater fisheries including

data collection programs for catch and effort statistics in both marine and inland fisheries, stock assessment and enhanced

scientific knowledge of biodiversity and of the contribution of protected areas to aquatic ecosystems. The activity will also

include training of scientific staff (training courses, scholarships for high-level academic training), support for the

rehabilitation of existing research resources (e.g., research vessel, laboratories) and acquisition of additional research

equipment. This activity will be led by CNSHB with technical assistance from the French National Research Institute for

Sustainable Development (Institut de Recherche pour le Développement, IRD).

33.      Promoting climate-smart innovations in fisheries/aquaculture sectors includes acquiring pilot solar-powered

refrigerated containers to preserve catch and combat post-harvest losses, carrying out studies to improve gas use

efficiency for motorized fishing boats and piloting resource-efficient smoking ovens.

text:
million equivalent AFD). This sub-component aims to strengthen small-scale fisheries value chains (both maritime and

inland) and improve sanitary conditions in fish processing and cold chain storage. Interventions will focus on enhancing

value chain efficiency by increasing access to infrastructure, reducing post-harvest losses, and expanding market access.

38.     Climate-resilient and gender-informed infrastructure for small scale fisheries. The project will support the

construction or rehabilitation of five31 integrated landing sites for small-scale maritime fisheries and one landing site for

inland small-scale fisheries. Site specific infrastructures will include wharfs, coastal protection infrastructure (e.g., dikes),

waste and wastewater management, access roads, smoking ovens, rehabilitation of processing sites, facilities for

fishermen and fishmongers (gear stores, workshops, ice plants), quarters for supervising authorities (CNSP, ONSPA) and

childcare facilities. The project will consult with women during technical studies to ensure the proposed infrastructure

meets their needs. A support program will then be implemented to ensure these infrastructures benefit women and

involve them in management and local governance (see paragraph 27).

39.     Sanitary improvements. The project will support the sanitary monitoring and control operations of fisheries value

chains by providing technical and operational support to ONSPA. This includes developing inspection and certification

protocols, creating an information system for traceability of inspections and certificates, constructing ONSPA

headquarters, and building and equipping a reference laboratory for the analysis of fishery products.

40.     Training of national maritime professionals. The project will also improve national resources for academic and

practical training of maritime professionals, including artisanal and industrial fishing personnel (a requirement to develop

a national cadre of maritime professionals as well as fishery observers on international fleets), though provision of

technical assistance to the national maritime school (Centre de Formation Professionnelle Maritime, CFPM) for the

development of training courses adapted to the needs and provision of training equipment.

relevant stakeholders by providing training and equipment to ANAG, launching a national aquaculture research-action

43.    Key infrastructure for aquaculture development. The project will invest in the construction of four aquaculture

hubs, which will include key infrastructure such as hatcheries, a demonstration feed production facility, and aquaculture

education centers. These hubs aim to enhance the provision of extension services and ensure a critical mass of well-trained

and equipped public and private sector extension providers to support the intensification of aquaculture in the country.

44.     Sustainable production of local aquaculture feed. The project will promote the sustainable production of local

aquaculture feed by utilizing local agricultural by-products and alternatives to animal meal. This will be achieved by

providing technical assistance to investors through ANAG and supporting research centers and NGOs.

45.     In addition to these project activities, AFD will contribute to the development of aquaculture through parallel

financing of US$4.4 million equivalent for the ‘’Kounki C2D project.’’ This funding is dedicated to family based agro-

ecological fish farming in four intervention zones: Southern and Northern Forest Guinea, Southern Upper Guinea and

Piedmont and Mangrove Zone in Maritime Guinea. This “Kounki C2D project’’ aims to improve the resilience and

performance of family farms by integrating sustainable and profitable fish farming models that are adapted to the climatic,

physical, economic and social conditions of these areas, while maintaining active fish farming operations in these four

zones.

fisheries and aquaculture sectors. It will support the establishment of a PPCG mechanism for aquaculture and fisheries

within Guinean guarantee fund for MSMEs (Fonds de Garantie des Prêts aux Entreprises, FGPE).33 The aim is to develop

access to credit from financial institutions for fishers and fish farmers by mitigating the credit risk for lending institutions.

Activities will include capital endowment for the dedicated fisheries and aquaculture window within the FGPE (US$5

million) and provision of technical assistance to the FGPE and other financial institutions to analyze and manage loans and

market new products tailored to the targeted sectors.34 Moreover, as women entrepreneurs have even more limited

access to finance, a dedicated technical assistance will support female-led MSMEs, through gender inclusive consultations

and targeted trainings, to develop their business plan and bankable credit applications to help them establish and/or grow

their businesses. The PPCG's procedure manual will also ensure that female-led MSMEs are eligible for the mechanism.

     19. BOOST-YOU will scale proven approaches and introduce new elements to Somalia’s social protection system to

     expand its impact on long-term resilience against climate-induced shocks and other types of shocks, and productivity

     focusing on building inclusive and sustainable jobs of today and jobs of the future. Building on the foundational blocks

     established through SNHCP and SNLRP, the proposed project will leverage the analytical work under the Somalia Social

     Protection Programmatic Advisory Services and Analytics (PASA): Building an Adaptive National Social Protection System

     (P500503) and scale up proven approaches based on lessons from past programs. Key investments in social registry

     development, digital payment systems, and delivery mechanisms have laid a robust foundation for expanding coverage

     and enhancing government-led social protection programming. These systems are designed to enable integrated

     support across sectors, linking social protection with health, education, nutrition, climate adaptation, emergency

     preparedness and management, and labor market interventions to promote human capital accumulation and future

     employment. In addition, the project will further expand economic inclusion measures to support youth employment,

     addressing both supply- and demand-side barriers to jobs and promoting climate-resilient livelihoods while also

     strengthening human capital linkages by further improving uptake of available education, health and nutrition services.

     Recognizing the role of social protection in breaking intergenerational cycles of poverty, and as a catalyst for inclusive

     labor force participation, these innovations will contribute to a more sustainable and inclusive development trajectory.

     The financing will be processed under paragraph 12 of Section III of the Investment Project Financing Policy: Projects in

     Situations of Urgent Need of Assistance or Capacity Constraints. The project is proposed to run over a period of four

     years, with a closing date on December 31, 2029.

     20. The project is fully Paris Agreement-aligned with global climate adaptation and mitigation goals and with

     Somalia’s commitments under its Nationally Determined Contribution (2021) and National Adaptation Programme of

     Action (2013). By ratifying the Paris Climate Agreement, United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, and

     Kyoto Protocol, Somalia has demonstrated its commitment to building climate resilience and pursuing a sustainable

     development pathway. Regarding adaptation, the project strengthens national delivery systems, shock-responsive cash

     transfers, and human capital interventions to address the main climate and disaster risks—droughts, floods, and extreme

     heat events. These risks are unlikely to materially impact the achievement of the PDO, given that delivery mechanisms

     are designed to be flexible, scalable, and geographically responsive. BOOST-You’s investments in systems and capacities

     help climate-proof social protection and contribute meaningfully to adaptation as investments in systems and capacities

     are expected to result in a national adaptive social protection system to enable rapid provision of emergency cash

     transfers anywhere in the country. The use of the distress index, combined with the geospatial functionality of the USR

     ensures that geographic targeting reflects exposure to climatic shocks and vulnerability levels. Household data collected

     through the National Socio-Economic Survey and the USR includes information on climate-dependent livelihoods,

     enhancing the ability to assess climate vulnerability and respond effectively during crises. The project’s support for

     emergency cash transfers, as well as for economic inclusion interventions tailored to build resilient livelihoods for youth

     and women, helps reduce reliance on negative coping strategies—such as environmentally harmful practices like

     charcoal production—and supports longer-term adaptation. Regarding mitigation, the project has no significant

     greenhouse gas emissions and does not negatively affect Somalia’s low-carbon development pathway. Its focus on

     poverty reduction, resilience building, and inclusive economic opportunities is fully consistent with mitigation objectives

     under the Paris Agreement. The project has been screened for climate and disaster risk. In sum, BOOST-You makes an

     important contribution to strengthening institutional and household-level resilience to climate shocks, supporting

     Somalia’s transition from crisis response to long-term, climate-resilient development.

     21. This dual approach—scaling what works and innovating for impact—will reinforce the transition from

     humanitarian relief to long-term development programming, ensuring that social protection investments contribute

     to sustainable and equitable economic growth. By combining expanded proven interventions and new climate-sensitive

     approaches, BOOST-YOU will further strengthen Somalia’s adaptive, inclusive, and government-led social protection

     system, ensuring that social protection becomes a key enabler of jobs, human capital development, and economic

     inclusion and is aligned with the World Bank’s vision for achieving universal social protection.

     22. BOOST-YOU consists of three components, each contributing to the PDO: 1) Connecting Youth and Women to

     Better Jobs Today; 2) Investing in People for Better Jobs Tomorrow; and 3) Adaptive Social Protection Systems and

     Project Management.

title: Unconditional Cash Transfers (US$13.5 million equivalent).
text:
28. This subcomponent provides unconditional cash transfers to households that are chronically poor and

     vulnerable living in climate-vulnerable areas in order to bolster human capital outcomes, strengthen climate

     resilience, and lay the groundwork for future employment readiness in the context of deep climate vulnerability. The

     objectives of the component are to (a) support households to strengthen their resilience, avoid negative coping

     practices, and meet escalating needs consequent to climate shocks including droughts and floods in the short term and

     (b) protect and promote human capital accumulation21 and climate resilience in the medium to long term by continuing

     to smooth consumption gaps through predictable and reliable cash transfers. The design includes measures to ensure

     that female-headed households and women within male-headed households are prioritized as the main cash transfer

     recipient, contributing to narrowing gender gaps in access to financial resources, reducing their heightened climate

     vulnerability and supporting women’s economic empowerment as a pathway to more inclusive job creation in the future.

     These cash transfers directly contribute to increased consumption of health, nutrition, and education services which

     improves productive labor participation while providing them enhancing beneficiaries’ adaptive capacity to climate

     shocks. Cash transfers improve resilience to shocks by preventing use of negative coping strategies such as distress

     migration and depletion of productive assets. By smoothing consumption in areas affected by recurrent climate shocks,

     they also contribute to reducing the risk of school dropouts and protecting maternal and child health outcomes.

     29. The subcomponent will finance unconditional cash transfers (UCT) delivered through mobile payments of US$20

     per month to women head of households from 50,000 of the poorest households (Cohort 2 of the FGS’s Baxnaano

     program, approximately 300,000 individuals selected under SNHCP) for a period of one additional year.22 The cohort has

     been selected under SNHCP, using a combination of geographical DDI based and PMT based targeting using the USR.

     These geo-spatially informed tools will help ensure that areas vulnerable to climate change impacts are prioritized for

     support. The subcomponent will build on implementation arrangements piloted under SNHCP: Enrollment, payments,

     and grievance redress will continue to be managed directly by the government through Baxnaano’s newly developed

     national Social Protection Delivery System (SPDS). In addition, MoLSA will retain a payment service provider, a

     communication and beneficiary mobilization firm, and a third-party monitoring firm throughout the duration of

     implementation. Citizen feedback through the Grievance Redress Mechanism (GRM) will be actively used to identify and

     address inclusion and service quality issues.

     30. In addition, beneficiaries under the project will also be linked to skill trainings offered the Empowering Women

     through Education and Skills Project (Rajo Kaaba, P176898). A referral mechanism will be created to establish linkages

     for Baxnaano beneficiaries located in Rajo Kaaba supported districts. This integrated approach connects social protection

     and skills development to enhance employability of vulnerable populations that experience a heightened vulnerability

     to climate hazards. The combination of cash and skills may become a prelude to a comprehensive graduation program

     in the future, supporting long-term transitions from poverty to climate-resilient productive employment. Trainings

     provided will include modules on climate-resilient livelihoods and promote women’s economic empowerment, aligning

     social protection measures with broader jobs and climate adaptation goals.

title: Human Capital Co-Responsibility Cash Transfers (US$17.2million equivalent).
text:
31. This subcomponent provides human capital linked CCTs to 30,000 pregnant women and mothers of children

     between 0-2 years of age in selected districts and introduces a pilot that would support 5,000 children improve uptake

     of primary education services in one district over four years. Gender-responsive design will ensure these interventions

     address barriers women face in accessing maternal health and education services for their children, while strengthening

     resilience to climate shocks that disrupt access to these services and have negative impacts on human capital outcomes.

     BOOST-YOU prioritizes CCTs in line with global evidence and lessons from SNHCP demonstrating the effectiveness of soft

     nudges in sustaining behavior change in settings where opportunity costs and adoption of negative coping strategies by

     households are high. A combination of Baxnaano’s SPDS, MoLSA’s partnerships with Ministries of Health and Education,

     and newly established TPM capacity have made reliable verification of compliance possible. Tying transfers to objectively

     verifiable behaviors—such as participation in health awareness sessions at health facilities and school attendance—

for one year. Subject to resource availability, through the Somalia Multi-partner Fund, or International Development Association, additional

     targets high-return human capital investments, reinforces climate-resilient practices, and builds a healthier, better-

     educated, and more productive future workforce. Conditionalities will be enforced only where services are available and

     can be suspended during major climate or access disruptions.

     32. Health & Nutrition Co-Responsibility Cash Transfer (H&N CCT) – This subcomponent will enable continued

     operations and provision of services through existing Baxnaano Facilitation Centers which have been tested under

     SNHCP. H&N CCT targets the poorest 20-25 percent households (using USR generated PMT targeting lists) in selected

     districts with pregnant women and mothers of children between 0-2 years selected as prime beneficiaries.23 This CCT

     directly mitigates adverse health and nutrition impacts caused by or exacerbated by climate change induced shocks.

     Beneficiaries are provided all CCT and related health services at Baxnaano Facilitation Centers, established within existing

     health facilities. At facilitation centers, eligible beneficiaries are enrolled, receive health and nutrition awareness sessions

     that integrate messaging on how to protect child and maternal health during climate hazard exposure such as droughts,

     floods and extreme heat (including heat stress, waterborne diseases, and sanitation practices), and growth monitoring.

     The participation in these sessions also constitutes the co-responsibility that needs to be satisfied to receive US$30 per

     quarter through mobile payments. In addition, beneficiaries are encouraged to receive vaccination services, receive

     referral services to stabilization centers (in case of significant acute malnutrition with complications), avail malnutrition

     treatment therapies and receive Multi-Micronutrient Supplementation. During implementation, the use of facilitation

     centers as one-stop-shop service delivery platforms will be explored. District selection prioritizes highly climate-shock

     affected areas and areas hosting displaced populations. Baxnaano Facilitation centers will also provide climate-sensitive

     health messaging, including guidance on management of maternal and child health during drought and flood

     emergencies, linking human capital investments with climate resilience and future labor productivity.

     33. Education Co-responsibility Cash Transfer (ECCT) – A pilot ECCT initiative will support 5,000 children from the

     poorest households in one district of Somalia.24 District selection requires presence of adequate supply of education

     services, accessibility, overlap with UCT districts, and use of USR/PMT to identify eligible households. ECCT aims to

     increase enrollment of school-age children, improve attendance rates for children in primary education and reduce drop-

     out rates, laying the educational foundation critical for future employability and inclusion in productive jobs. The co-

     responsibilities include (a) enrolment of eligible children in a participating school and (b) at least 70 percent attendance

     for each child during a quarter. This attendance threshold is designed to counteract common negative coping

     strategies—such as child labor or school withdrawal—often adopted during periods of climate-induced shocks,

     displacement, or climate-exacerbated food insecurity. Upon compliance with co-responsibilities, eligible beneficiary

     households receive US$30 per quarter through mobile payments. The intervention leverages World Food Programme’s

     (WFP) longstanding partnership with MoLSA to prioritize qualification of schools being supported through World Bank’s

     Rajo Kaaba and WFP’s school feeding program. Baxnaano will implement mobilization and awareness, enrolment

     facilitation and confirmation, quarterly attendance monitoring, regular spot checks and quality assurance, in

     coordination with the Ministry of Education. Community mobilization efforts will prioritize inclusion of girls and children

     with disabilities who experience a heightened vulnerability to climate hazards. Enrollment, payments, and grievance

     redress will continue to be managed directly by the government through Baxnaano’s SPDS. In addition, MoLSA will retain

     a payment service provider, a communication and beneficiary mobilization firm, a security firm, and a TPM firm

     throughout the duration of implementation.

title: Shock Responsive Cash Transfers (US$4 million equivalent, including US$2 million from GSFF).
text:
34. This subcomponent finances emergency cash transfers in response to future climate-related shocks. There is

     substantial global evidence on the impact of emergency cash transfers. This includes offsetting reductions in human

     capital, enabling early recovery and preventing adoption of negative coping strategies that cause permanent loss of

     welfare, which in turn help protect the human capital base needed for future livelihood recovery and job readiness. With

     support from the GSFF, this subcomponent establishes a pre-arranged ECT funding mechanism with a trigger model. Key

     features of this activity include: (a) development of clear, predetermined triggers based on climate and food security

     indicators that, when met, would automatically release funds for emergency cash transfers; (b) establishment of robust

     governance mechanism for a contingent funding mechanism with clear linkages to disaster risk financing mechanism

     managed by the government; (c) creation of a framework to crowd in other humanitarian funds, leveraging the GSFF

     contribution to attract additional resources from humanitarian partners; and (d) establishment of protocols for rapid

     deployment of emergency cash transfers to affected populations within days of a trigger event. This pre-arranged

     funding mechanism would significantly enhance the project's ability to respond swiftly to crises, providing immediate

     support to vulnerable populations when they need it most. Enabling rapid decision making through agreed Standard

     Operating Procedures (SOPs), contingent funding and a robust delivery system, the project can dramatically reduce the

     time between the onset of a climate shock and the delivery of assistance. Linkages with early warning systems for

     geographical targeting will require close coordination with the Somalia Disaster Management Agency (SoDMA) and will

     be developed in partnership with the De-Risking, Inclusion and Value Enhancement of Pastoral Economies (DRIVE,

     P176517) Project. The activity will be based on learnings from the micro-level triggers used under DRIVE to inform

     The subcomponent will support provision of ECTs to 10,000 climate-shock affected households selected using a

     combination of geo-spatial analysis and PMT based targeting,25 delivering US$60 per month for a period of six months

     through mobile payments in beneficiaries specialized limited mandate wallets.

title: Adaptive Social Protection Systems (US$6.5 million equivalent).
text:
36. This subcomponent will support institutional strengthening and capacity development of the government’s

     Somalia SPP (Baxnaano), enabling formalized government led social protection service delivery. In addition, the

     subcomponent supports the social registry, social protection delivery systems and improved institutional capabilities in

     Somalia (including Somaliland). The project will provide dedicated support for capacity building, ensuring that concerned

     line ministries26 are well-equipped to manage and oversee multiple social protection programs effectively and to

     coordinate these with human capital and jobs agendas. The investment into SPDS enhances adaptive social protection

     and improves flexibility to accommodate changes necessitated by the evolving security situation and climate change by

     leveraging technology, ensuring full portability of benefits and maximizing reach, particularly for climate shock response.

     37. The adaptive SPDS aims to create a rapid ECT delivery mechanism to ensure efficient and effective government-

     led implementation using USR data and the payment mechanism established through SNHCP. Targeting using geo-

     spatial analysis, objective vulnerability-based prioritization and categorical targeting criteria (with a special consideration

     for climate-related vulnerabilities) will lead to generation of targeting lists from the USR. Linkages with early warning

     systems for geographical targeting will be supported to guide the government’s response to extreme-weather events.

     This will require close coordination with SoDMA. SPDS will continue to track gender-disaggregated data, climate

     vulnerability indicators, and enable feedback loops from communities to improve targeting of both social protection and

     job-linked interventions in future shocks.

     38. For the USR, the development of an On-Demand Registration (ODR) mechanism represents a critical innovation

     in Somalia's social protection landscape. This mechanism will be designed and tested under the project, leveraging

     technology to reduce dependence on field deployment for data collection and enable on-demand updates/registration;

     Some level of field presence will be considered to manage updates as part of ODR and deal with issues of communication

     and grievances. The project will support deployment of ODR within government systems to create an efficient and

     responsive system for maintaining up-to-date information on existing beneficiaries and potential beneficiaries, crucial

     for targeting and delivering social protection interventions, especially in case of climate change induced shocks.

title: National Socio-economic Survey (US$30.5 million equivalent).
text:
39. This subcomponent will finance the National Socio-Economic Survey for the USR which was initially supported

     under SNHCP. As the survey will require between 18-24 months for completion, the government requested that the

     survey be considered under BOOST-You to allow adequate time for its implementation. A pilot survey to register 200,000

     households is being undertaken by the government with support from WFP and its data collection partner using the

     government’s USR data collection application and tool, USR operational guidelines, protocols and systems under SNHCP.

     The NSES is a critical investment in strengthening climate change adaptability by enabling the rapid and technology-

     enabled identification of households most affected by climate-related shocks. Leveraging socio-economic data in the

     USR, geospatial analysis and early warning systems, the project will allow the government to swiftly target and deliver

     assistance to shock affected vulnerable populations experiencing extreme weather events. Leveraging technology and

     digital services across social protection systems will enable rapid updates, minimize delays and enable the government

     to support households whose livelihoods and food security are most at risk across the country.

     40. The NSES will conduct nationwide27 field data collection activities for gathering biometric backed socioeconomic

     information on all accessible households and their members in Somalia. Collection of data on a household and its

     members results in their registration in the USR. The survey will lead to collection of socio-economic data for

     approximately 2 million accessible households (approximately 12,000,000 individuals) across Somalia. Registration of

     the population in the USR enables improved targeting of the poor and vulnerable through the generation of welfare

     scores using a PMT. This targeting approach maximizes returns on the government’s pro-poor investment by enhancing

     speed, accuracy, transparency, and efficiency. The survey is a strategic investment which enables Baxnaano to respond

     with ECTs to climate change-induced shocks anywhere in Somalia, improves the government’s ability to develop pro-

     poor policies, and significantly improves operational efficiency of social protection programs and humanitarian support

     in the country. MoLSA’s capacity to manage the USR has been strengthened under SNHCP and further complemented

MoLSA has also strengthened the governance of the USR by establishing a USR Oversight Board to oversee data privacy,

protection, and sharing through Ministerial Decree. In addition, data protection, management, security, and privacy

arrangements have also been strengthened. An independent Data Protection Advisor will be appointed by MoLSA,

41. The survey will be launched in two districts of each FMS and territory at the same time. Upon registration of all

households in the initial districts, survey teams will await completion of quality assurance activities prior to moving to

the next districts. The quality assurance process undertaken by a third-party re-collects data from 10 percent of

households in each sub-district for comparison with survey data. In case there is a variation of more than ten percent

42. The project will also support MoLSA’s collaboration with the National Identification and Registration Authority

(NIRA), which is supported through the SPRING project. Collaboration with NIRA will be critical to accelerate the

issuance of national identification documents for beneficiaries registered in the USR. Linking USR registration with the

deliver benefits securely and efficiently, particularly during shock responses when timely verification is essential.

title: Basic Package of Nutrition Services (US$48.85 million)
text:
26. Component 1 will support Nigeria’s response to the acute food security and nutrition crisis by delivering essential

nutrition services at scale to protect vulnerable populations. It builds on the ANRiN Project’s deployment of a BPNS

through a continuation of the community-based service delivery model, using performance-based contracts with non-

state actors and behavior change interventions. Services were selected based on proven national and international

evidence on the most cost-effectiveness and feasibility of urgent deployment under crisis circumstances. With

malnutrition rates rising, interventions have been prioritized for immediate expansion at health facilities. Additional

financing was leveraged by Kaduna State to provide good-quality health and nutrition services to married adolescents to

enable birth spacing initiatives, and to provide ready-to-use therapeutic foods (RUTF) for treating severe acute

malnutrition (to treat SAM) in children aged 6–59 months.

title: Convergence with Food Systems (US$24.80 million)
text:
32. Component 2 will support the scale-up of homestead gardens in states that are in the IPC crisis phase, yielding

an enhanced and diverse production system centered around nutrient-rich crops and small livestock. Leveraging a

review of historic homestead and micro-gardening activities in Nigeria, including from the ANRiN Project, and prevailing

weather information, a compendium of priority crops and small livestock will be adapted for each geographic area,

including dry/wet season-specific packages. This component will adopt home-based consumption as the primary

objective whilst promoting an income-generation pathway. A study on the nutrient gap in Nigeria revealed that actual

diets are heavier in staples and lacking in more micronutrient-rich fruits, vegetables, legumes, and nuts. The findings

also showed that more than 50 percent of rural households relied on markets to acquire food. 35 Indicatively, the rising

costs of food and transportation, coupled with households’ lower purchasing power, will make it more difficult for

Nigerian households to afford nutritious diets. Finally, the study revealed that children aged 12–23 months are less likely

to be fed fruits, vegetables, legumes, and nuts, even when these are available, indicating suboptimal complementary

feeding for this physiologically vulnerable group and calling for a shift in intra-household norms around food distribution.

A diverse homestead gardening effort will be an important factor in reversing these trends.



Sub-component 2. 1 Establishment of Homestead Gardens (US$17.20 million)



33. This sub-component will scale up mixed demonstration farms and homestead gardens to improve household

access to and affordability of a nutritious diet for all age groups. Individual homestead gardens will be targeted to

1,000-day households, including female-headed households and those with adolescent mothers, which make up 3.6

percent and 24.2 percent of households in the NSR. Community gardens or demonstration farms will be prioritized for

women owner and cultivator clusters. A variety of micronutrient-rich crops, including fruits, vegetables (such as

eggplant, okra, peppers, and beans), iron-rich leafy greens, tubers (such as orange-fleshed sweet potatoes), legumes,

and marketable produce (such as tomatoes, onions, carrots, and cabbage) will be cultivated. Small livestock like goats
