and poultry (for example, noilier chickens), which are more resistant and adaptable and thus reduce vulnerability to

climate-related shocks will also be provided to diversify household access to animal protein sources. Other neglected

tropical crops with the potential to provide food, nutrition, and income (such as Bambara nuts) will also be explored.

Animal feed will be customized to fit the local environment.



34. Agricultural input kits will be designed around short-duration (<90 days), high-yield crop varieties with

adaptability to thrive in diverse ecological and environmental conditions, with the aim of helping to surmount the

challenges posed by variable weather patterns. This will be particularly useful during the lean season when families are

likely to fall back on calorie-dense foods such as bulky carbohydrates rather than addressing all nutrient requirements.

Micro-irrigation equipment, including drip irrigation from wells in demonstration farms and household gardens, will also

be critical to address the challenges of variable precipitation and support dry-season farming. Depending on the layout

of villages, homestead gardens will be created near homes or on the outskirts of villages. If the group has a community

farm, it will be divided into sections for the demonstration farm and for each beneficiary in the group. The mixed

approach will ensure ongoing food production throughout the year, with crop selections adjusted to seasonal changes

(rainy and dry seasons), while creating spaces for raising poultry and small livestock. Priority extension services will

include input bundles (including seeds, tools, and fertilizers), water management (to empower homestead gardeners to

optimize the use of available water sources, reduce waste, and promote sustainable gardening practices), and MIYCN

counseling. Strategies will include the implementation of rainwater harvesting systems and the promotion of

appropriate irrigation methods, soil conservation (including mulching, weeding, cover-cropping, and crop rotation), and

pest management.



35. The training and extension services component will build on the current homestead gardening, food processing,

and perseveration manuals developed under the ANRiN Project, which will be updated to be more context-responsive

and climate-smart based on additional mapping. Modules on: (a) available nutrients per serving; (b) the economics of

production (including input requirements and costs); (c) labor effort; (d) agricultural management practices; (e) duration

to maturity; (f) expected yield; (g) profitability; (h) making allowances for household consumption; (i) marketing and

income generation; and (j) MIYCN counseling, will be refined and included in the implementation guide for agricultural

extension agents, community health extension agents, and other technical project implementers. The integration of the

food processing and perseveration modules will help prevent post-harvest losses and improper disposal of food waste,

which can contribute to Greenhouse Gass (GHG) emissions whilst incorporation of light market-access support will boost

the income generation objective.



36. Interventions will focus on closing the gender gap. Data suggests that women have a subordinate position in the

value chain and markets. 36 Although women contribute 40 to 60 percent of agricultural labor and manage 60 to 90

percent of processing tasks, only few own land. Women receive less than 10 percent of available credit and grapple with

multiple non-work demands. Poverty restricts their ability to buy improved seedlings, fertilizers, and other farm inputs,

resulting in the cultivation of lower-value crops and 30 percent lower production per hectare than men. Equal access to

resources for women could boost agricultural yields by 20 to 30 percent. 37 At the same time, women—especially during

pregnancy—and adolescent girls have significant dietary needs. It is anticipated that the demonstration farms and

homestead gardens will yield sufficient produce to meet dietary needs and generate marketable surpluses for local

markets, enhancing food security and boosting incomes, especially among women. Additionally, it will increase women’s

title: Data-Driven Multisectoral Coordination and Accountability (US$6.35 million)
text:
38. This component aims to enhance critical coordination and accountability functions at both the national and state

levels. The Federal Ministry of Budget and Economic Planning (FMBEP) will lead the multisectoral coordination to address

the food and nutrition security crisis and to ensure that all implementing entities are held accountable. Component 3 will

prioritize three subcomponents.

title: Modified Basic Package of Nutrition Services (US$40.00 million)
text:
27. Subcomponent 1.1 will ensure availability of preventive and life-saving commodities leveraging existing

deployment platforms to deliver micronutrient powders, deworming and Zn-ORS. It will enhance BPNS will support to

include small-quantity lipid-based nutrient supplements (SQ-LNS) and RUTF for prevention and treatment, respectively,

of SAM. SQ-LNS helps prevent stunting and anemia in children 6-23 months. Some interventions in the BPNS are already

financed through other resources, such as VAS and multiple micronutrient supplementation (MMS) for pregnant women

but will nonetheless be delivered complementarily as part of a comprehensive package. The BPNS will continue to be

delivered at the community level by public sector CHW. This approach will leverage the Primary Healthcare Provision

Strengthening Program (P504693) 30 and the Nigeria Human Capital Opportunities for Prosperity and Equity–Governance

(P181476) 31 programs to institutionalize CHWs. At the health facility level, the BPNS will continue to offer the same suite

of services. ANRiN 2.0 will adopt a coordinated procurement approach for all nutrition services.



28. The design of the enhanced BPNS makes use of data from the most recent Nigeria Demographic and Health Survey

(NDHS) 2023 to optimize available resources to achieve multiple objectives. Geospatial Optima Nutrition analyses were

conducted to ensure efficient allocation of the additional resources across the first 13 states, as well as all 21 states, and

within the enhanced BPNS. The analyses optimized the package with the objective of maximizing the number of alive,

non-wasted, and non-stunted children in a five-year period (2024–2028) with US$65 million in additional funding annually.

Optimizing the enhanced BPNS in 20 states would result in 260,000 fewer child deaths, 275,000 fewer children stunted,

55,000 fewer children wasted, and an overall reduction in stunting prevalence by 2.6 percentage points over the five-year

period.



29. The suggested distribution of additional funds indicates a need to reallocate resources to states with a higher

disease burden where current per-capita spending is inadequate (Figure 2). For example, it is optimal to allocate more

Niger, and Zamfara). The model also considered state-specific breastfeeding distributions, health system attendance, and

These interventions largely prevent wasting and stunting by reducing diarrhea incidence and improving birth outcomes.

The analyses also suggested allocating funds toward the treatment of severe and moderate acute malnutrition, but only

after funds were used for preventive services. This highlights the need to ensure that interventions to address the food

and nutrition security crises include prevention activities.

39. This sub-component will ensure an expansion of the Nutrition-Responsive Public Financial Management by scaling

up the Budget Tagging and Tracking System in all 36 states of the federation. Working with the Budget Office of the

Federation and the Office of the Accountant General, the FMBEP will coordinate the budget tagging process at the federal

level, ensuring the federal Ministries, Departments and Agencies (MDAs) allocate, tag, and track funding for nutrition with

additional emphasis on gender and climate-related activities. To replicate the system at subnational level, the State

Ministries of Budget and Economic Planning will be supported through the existing collaboration between FMBEP and the

Nigeria Governors’ Forum, on state nutrition financing efforts. This builds on the harmonized federal-state taxonomy

currently being utilized by the initial 11 ANRiN states whilst aligning between federal and state Charts of Accounts. This

system will help to identify resources, prioritize and monitor nutrition and climate funding in budget proposals and

releases, and determine spending gaps to allow for necessary adjustments. By integrating nutrition tagging into the

national budget cycle, this sub-component will improve resource mobilization and align it with nutrition and climate policy

priorities, ultimately providing better data for future nutrition investments. Budget tagging and tracking will also enhance

the efficiency and equity of financing, leading to greater provider accountability and improved outcomes.

title: Access to sustainable and climate resilient water and sanitation services (US$72.10 million
text:
equivalent). The component will support a combination of interventions from source to tap to strengthen the climate

resilience and sustainability of urban water supply and sanitation services that are regularly affected by climate-change-

exacerbated droughts and floods events, contributing to the implementation of priority climate-adaptation investments

enacted in the country’s NDC, specifically under the water resources and resilient water supply and sanitation systems

strategic area. The component is structured in five sub-components, specifically:

       (a) Reducing climate hazards impacting water supply infrastructure and services through Integrated Water

           Resources Management (IWRM) and watershed management (US$2.85 million equivalent), including

                 providing strategic support to ARA-Sul to fulfill its mandate, covering investments that will contribute to

                 strengthening of climate-informed water planning and allocation, the enhancement of water quality through

                 improved watershed management that reduces climate-change-exacerbated water-source contamination,

                 assurance of water availability to meet urban demand via source diversification, and demand conservation.

           (b) Expansion of access to climate-resilient water supply services (US$49.60 million equivalent), including

               investments for the expansion of water treatment and transmission capacity and related compensation costs,

               as well as downstream investments to expand the distribution network following the key principles for

               climate-resilient water infrastructure design. These include key water treatment plant (WTP) investments to

               tap alternative sources to improve the climate resilience of services by reducing dependence on a single

               source; and pumping stations and bridge crossings for main pipes designed to withstand and be installed

               above historic flood levels—some of the recommended hard and soft measures for climate-proofing of water-

               supply infrastructure and service.25

           (c) Output-based payments (OBP) for low-income household connections (US$6.50 million equivalent),

               building on the successful experience of output-based payments implemented in WASIS II (P149377), aims at

               increasing access to piped water connections for low-income households in the main urban centers. Under

               this sub-component, output-based grant payments are to be provided to regional utilities to cover the costs

               of connecting low-income households.

           (d) Improvement of the quality of services provided by PWPs (US$7.65 million equivalent) through grants for

               upgrading PWP water supply infrastructure to comply with technical standards, with best practices for

               climate-proofing of operations and service, and to enable them to distribute bulk water purchased from the

               regional utilities.

           (e) Access to safely managed sanitation (US$5.50 million equivalent) financing the completion of the ongoing

               Fecal Sludge Treatment Plant in Tete currently supported by the MUSP (P161777), which will close in

               September 2025, and to support the strengthening of fecal sludge management practices in urban areas of

               Mozambique. These activities will reduce the contamination of water bodies and groundwater, as well as soil,

               thereby also lowering the potential impact of floods (from contaminated floodwaters).
